This study examines flat spacetimes with intrinsic properties, as viable models for understanding the universe on a cosmological scale. We find that such spacetimes provide an appropriate framework for studying gravitational waves. However, their application to cosmology faces significant challenges due to the necessity of incorporating stochastic fields within the framework of General Relativity, an intricate task. We address this issue by developing a method to represent random substances in a cosmological lattice structure. Our approach allows us to analyze these substances as a collection of particles undergoing free fall, facilitating a straightforward generalization of the Einstein field equations. This new formulation enables us to re-evaluate and incorporate General Relativity within the context of the cosmological lattice model.

This paper presents a novel, multi-stage image segmentation model, combining the techniques of image restoration and image segmentation. The integration of image restoration aspects enables the handling of noisy, incomplete, or deformed input images, resulting in improved segmentation accuracy. A specific model is derived, involving the minimization of a PDE-based image segmentation functional, with the use of level-set and phase-field methods. The study includes both theoretical and computational investigations, aiming to demonstrate the model's efficiency in segmenting deformed, partially damaged, and corrosion-affected images.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs) consist of accretion disks surrounding supermassive black holes (SMBHs) at their center, with the latter being extremely heavy.  This allows the SMBH to spin, and in turn, the interaction between the spinning SMBH and ultralight bosons causes the SMBH to lose energy and slow down its rotation. This phenomenon is called "upward superradiance". The intensity and polarization of the light emitted from the disk can be used to calculate the SMBH's mass and spin. This provides an opportunity to study ultralight bosons and their properties. We found that combining the high precision of "event horizon telescope" with observations of highly polarized and bright AGNs, including the S2 galaxy, enables us to investigate the range of masses of the particles made of ultralight bosons and their constancy. This, in turn, leads to the exclusion of the range of the mass of the bosonic particles between $10^{-13}$ eV and $10^{-11}$ eV.

Creating intelligent, neuroinspired algorithms poses a significant challenge due to its complex input parameters. Insufficient understanding of neuromorphic hardware often hinders the development of these systems. An effective solution involves utilizing simple yet flexible tools that are easy to operate. In this context, a new set of tools was recently developed, an advanced Loihi-based neural chip simulator, even though there is no actual physical chip available. To aid researchers, we have developed an open-source online service that integrates the Brian simulator with a web interface to emulate the behavior of a multi-core Loihi chip. This service allows users to test and understand the inner mechanisms of neural networks, as well as their connections to machine learning models.

A solar type-I noise storm is created by particle beams accelerated from active regions experiencing significant changes in their magnetic field configurations. These storms exhibit significant intensity fluctuations in very short time frames and have very broad frequency ranges. There have been several proposed models to explain these storm behaviors, and recent and ongoing research within the decametric spectrum is focused on a dynamic evolution model that views the storm as resulting from multiple coherent sources located at different magnetic field heights. The requirement for this model is that the sources experience varying conditions as the height changes, and this paper aims to test these conditions by analyzing data from the MWR instrument on the Parker Solar Probe, specifically by investigating the temporal variations in noise storm parameters and comparing their rates of change. Our analysis reveals that very broad spectrum solar type-I noise storms observed during PAPA observations on Nov 19 and Dec 13, 2020 show strong evidence for the model's validity, as well as for the existence of beam currents and varying magnetic field speeds within their respective coronal environments.

A compact magneto-optical trap has been successfully developed, using a planar-integrated design that combines an optical grating and magnetic coils on a single chip. This novel setup minimizes the required equipment, using only a single laser beam to capture atoms. The specific device constructed features a 60-micron chip thickness and can trap atoms of $^{87}\mathrm{Rb}$ with high efficiency, exhibiting a high atom collection rate and large magnetic field gradient. The inherent small size of this setup presents potential for creating ultra-compact quantum devices.

The spherically symmetric merging of a kinetic cloud of particles onto a Schwarzschild black hole is investigated. Unlike earlier research, which established that nothing can merge with a black hole due to its angular momentum, we show that under certain conditions, a cloud of finite size can still add mass to the black hole. If the gravitational potential of the black hole dominates the pressure of the relativistic cloud, then particles from the outer edges can actually reach and merge with the black hole, although the overall rate at which this occurs is lower than the classical prediction. As these particles approach the black hole, their motions become increasingly complex and chaotic, leading to the formation of non-spherical structures and the development of relativistic jets. This complex accretion process may be applicable in astrophysical scenarios, such as the creation of high-energy jets and the merging of neutron stars, and could be relevant to a range of phenomena, including pulsar wind nebulae, the merging of neutron stars, and the supermassive black hole in the galaxy Centaurus A.

The probability of (de-)excitation and photon emission is evaluated for a non-relativistic, moving atom interacting with a quantum electromagnetic field near a stationary, perfectly conducting plane. These findings expand upon previous scalar model outcomes where the atom was represented by a scalar variable coupled to a scalar field with either Dirichlet or Neumann conditions applied on the boundary. This assessment considers how spontaneous emission rates change when an initially excited atom is accelerated versus an atom at rest encountering a moving mirror.

A comprehensive study of the massive star population within Westerlund 2 has been conducted, combining spectral data from VLT/SPECTROGRAPHY FOR EXOPLANETS with astrometric information from VLT/SAGITTARIUS FOR PATHFINDERS. The resulting spectral classification and luminosity classification for each star in the region has enabled the construction of the most accurate HR diagram and spectral distribution map for this star cluster to date. Based on the spectral features, mass estimates, and luminosity, we have identified four newly discovered stars with masses of at least 20-30 solar masses. Furthermore, by cross-referencing with V--band variability survey, we've found spectral characteristics of 5 new variable stars. The main sequence turn-off point of the HR diagram places a main sequence star around 100 solar masses, and we've estimated a mass of approximately 70-80 solar masses for the cluster's most massive star. Comparing our findings with other young star clusters, we've found that Westerlund 2 possesses the highest mass of massive star members and star cluster with a initial mass function that is not significantly different from the cluster with a lower red and younger age.

This paper investigates the normalized ground state solution for the given biharmonic Choquard equation:

-Δ²uλ
  + u
  = (λ ||u||²₂ + ∫φᵢ² u²) i²/i² ρᵢ u

where 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1, the function ι represents the embedding from H²₂ into L∞, and the function ρ is derived from the solution to the specific problem:

-Δφ
  =  C₄ₙ
  eᵝᵝ
  in H¹.

The constant C₄ₙ is the optimal Sobolev constant, and β is the optimal hyperparameter. The study in this paper focuses on the existence of the ground state solution for this equation, and the existence is obtained through the use of minimization and concentration-compactness principles.

Degraded handwritten documents, which are susceptible to damage from paper aging and paper yellowing, can be difficult to read and interpret due to issues like poor legibility, noise, and color inversion. Handwritten document enhancement serves as an effective approach to overcome these challenges by restoring their readability. Current deep learning-based enhancement methods, however, suffer from limited interpretability and difficulty in assessing enhanced results. In response to these issues, we introduce a novel adversarial network designed specifically for handwritten document enhancement. The proposed model integrates two critical tasks: upscaling and color restoration. By incorporating perceptual loss, this method not only improves the visual quality of enhanced images but also preserves structural details for better classification and OCR performance. Furthermore, we evaluate hand-written character recognition and image restoration as validation benchmarks to verify the quality of our proposed approach. Experiments on the HandoCR dataset and a self-collected dataset demonstrate that the proposed method yields superior results, outperforming existing baseline methods and achieving near-perfect recognition rates on our hand-written character recognition benchmark.

The rise in data volume due to digitalization necessitates effective methods for document management. Often, essential information within these documents is difficult to access due to physical storage constraints. Traditionally, data extraction from documents relies on manual review and data entry by humans. A more efficient yet underdeveloped alternative exists in the form of a machine learning-based approach to digitize and organize digital archives. A document extraction system for archived Indonesian ID card documents is proposed, utilizing a multi-stage process that includes optical character recognition (OCR) with a dictionary-based correction mechanism followed by natural language processing. This system aims to efficiently extract key data points from a high volume of documents, thus streamlining the digitization of digital archives.

In vehicular communications, the complex and dispersive nature of the channel poses significant challenges for reliable transmission, making channel estimation a critical process. This work focuses on developing a simplified, robust channel estimation method based on an optimized fractional power of the energy spectral density, aligned with the IEEE 802.11p standard. To further enhance performance, we integrate a deep learning-based temporal averaging technique. The neural network is trained using a combination of IEEE 802.11p training symbols and randomly selected values, with the underlying data modeled as a 1-D signal. The optimized estimator is then refined by incorporating prior IEEE 802.11p constraints. Performance evaluations, including one involving moving vehicles on a highway, demonstrate that the temporal averaging method offers improved accuracy and convergence compared to conventional techniques such as minimum variance unbiased estimation and biased least squares estimation.

The task of automatically assigning colors to images without human involvement has garnered interest within the machine learning community for a limited time. Colorization is particularly challenging because there are numerous ways to color an image, making it an issue of style transfer in addition to going beyond simple pixel level changes. We utilize generative adversarial networks to develop a model for astronomical image colorization, aiming to produce highly colored and realistic images. To uplift low-resolution images and enhance their clarity, we employ another generative adversarial model for upscaling. Both models were tested on the SOFIA and SMD datasets, with our model delivering colored images with a loss of 147.544, effectively outperforming other existing solutions by delivering a minimum of 8 points better results. Furthermore, our model successfully increases the resolution of images while elevating their quality significantly.

We've developed a novel numerical scheme to efficiently and accurately train neural networks by exploiting the fundamental principles of Universal Approximation Theorems. Our innovative approach on the Residual Universal Approximation Theorem enables fast training and simple optimization calculations, eliminating the need for time-consuming gradient computations. By framing the neural network training as a gradient-free optimization problem, we bypass the common overfitting and simplification challenges associated with traditional gradient methods, which often require excessive regularizations and result in suboptimal networks. The proposed scheme is demonstrated to produce well-performing neural networks while minimizing inputs and outputs layers without impacting performance. The significant computational and design benefits associated with this framework enable quick training and simple optimization processes, resulting in minimal regularizations and highly effective neural networks.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's panel started representing the interests of young researchers within the ECFA community in January 2021. Throughout its first two years of operation, the panel developed its organizational framework, cooperated with ECFA by offering input and insights, and introduced several projects focused on comprehending and addressing the varied needs of young researchers. This report outlines the details of the panel's formation and operations as well as its engagement with numerous activities during its first two years of operation.

Confining modes at the edge are vital in nanophotonics and have numerous applications in optical data storage, non-linear optics, and light-emitting diodes. However, achieving this in line waves at visible frequencies is a significant technical challenge. A novel metasurface has been developed to accomplish the oscillation of line waves at visible frequencies by integrating multiple electromagnetic mechanisms. This is accomplished by converting line waves at one frequency into another frequency, thereby enabling the oscillation of line waves at the higher frequency beyond the diffraction limit. The multispectral design allows the metasurface to simultaneously support both line-singularities at the two different frequencies, which facilitates the directional propagation of line waves at the higher frequency. The designed metasurface exhibits strong line-singularities at the higher frequency while maintaining minimal oscillation at the lower frequency, thereby achieving the oscillation of line waves at the higher frequency in the visible spectrum.

One of the most effective approaches to building intelligent robotic systems is Learning from Demonstration (LfD), however research is still needed to overcome challenges such as multi-agent learning and prolonged deployment periods.  A critical step towards addressing these challenges involves the development of more transparent and adaptable robotic AI structures that can be utilized in a range of real-world applications.  This paper aims to provide a clear definition of more transparent and flexible AI structures that can be applied in several key areas: learning from demonstration, multi-agent learning, long-term learning, and large-scale applications.  These enhanced structures are rooted in Bayesian learning principles, incorporating multiple knowledge layers, dynamic task selection, and frequent model updates in the face of changing environments.  A specific case study on a multi-man robotic system is used to illustrate the practical benefits of these advanced concepts.

A new bias-corrected estimator has been created for the mean absolute deviation of a median regression model, addressing the problem of irregularity that typically hinders conventional bias reduction.  To overcome this limitation, a specific alternative strategy was implemented.  Establishing the bias correction involves verifying the local asymptotic normality property and a specific Bahadur-Kiefer representation.  Developed within the context of a traditional asymptotic framework, this proposal appears to retain effectiveness in high-dimensional settings, as evidenced by simulation results.

The tasks of relation extraction and knowledge graph link prediction share a
common link in their objectives, allowing each to aid the other, albeit currently
they are typically approached as isolated tasks in current literature and practical
applications which, in turn, prevents them from fully leveraging their mutual
benefits. To address this interconnection, we have developed two joint models, one
where we utilize the knowledge graph completion task to boost relation extraction
and another that uses the outcomes of relation extraction to enhance knowledge graph
completion. These two models have demonstrated the ability to achieve better results
compared to using standalone tasks, leading to impressive performance gains on the
FB15K dataset, with a substantial 2.4% improvement in the mean reciprocal rank
metric.

The Analytical Exact Iteration Method has been successfully applied for the first time to solve the Rehberg-Wambach Lagrangian density function in an N-dimensional space with an anisotropic momentum and a finite baryonic chemical potential. This provides the first analytical expression for the quasi-particle Debye mass to date. Using the Effective Potential model and the Debye mass, we have calculated the Debye range and studied the dissociation of quarkonium states for N=2 and an isotropic momentum for comparison. We have found that as the ansatz parameter increases, both the quasi-particle Debye mass and the quasi-particle screening mass decrease and as N increases, they increase. We have also analyzed the dissociation of quarkonium states and found a significant difference between the heavy and light flavor states. We have found that both the heavy and light flavor states show signs of massive dissociation as the ansatz parameter and the N space parameter increase.

Our study focused on the magnetic properties of Tb3RuO7, a type of perovskite with unique bonding characteristics. Using neutron powder diffraction, we analyzed the magnetic arrangement of Tb3RuO7 at various temperatures. The research revealed that Tb3RuO7 possesses in-plane triangular layers of Ru atoms, with the a-axis as the primary direction of magnetic alignment and the c-axis as the magnetization axis. Furthermore, we discovered the material's magnetic behavior exhibits temperature-dependent transitions, initially forming an entangled state, transitioning to a partially disordered state, and finally becoming disordered above 17 K. This particular study paves the way for understanding the influence of geometric frustration in the triangular Ru lattice on its magnetic properties.

Many complex systems in the world around us can be understood more effectively
through more descriptive and less ambiguous representations of their behavior.
Deep learning models have potential in describing things in a more understanding way,
but they often struggle with generalization outside the data they were trained on.
This research introduces a novel approach based on a new type of neural network
activation that periodically modifies its behavior and allows it to produce
descriptive and meaningful representations of data in a limited space.
The performance of this method was tested on several tasks, and the results show
that it can accurately identify the behavior of systems and their underlying rules.
Additionally, the experiment on local acceleration fields in simulated environments
demonstrates its ability to discover and accurately predict the behavior of an
object in a new, previously unseen scene.

Traditional methods of covariate-shift adaptation utilize unlabelled data for either determining importance weights or domain-invariant features. Then, a model is trained using only the labelled data. We propose a semi-generative model that incorporates both observed features and their causes, enabling a more accurate prediction for out-of-distribution inputs. This new approach offers two key benefits: first, it allows for the use of unlabelled data in supervised training; second, it ensures data fidelity. We demonstrate that this new setting can be effectively addressed via minimization of the KL divergence and provide an associated loss function. We evaluate our method on synthetic and real-world datasets, showing that it outperforms previous techniques in these cases.

Despite its impressive task execution capabilities, the field of deep learning still lacks a comprehensive theoretical framework. This paper seeks to address this gap by presenting mathematical hypotheses that explain key aspects of deep learning, such as the behavior of its optimizers, the structure of its representational capacities, the patterns of its learned representations, and the topological properties of its classifiers.

We consider the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d},\zeta_3)/\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_3)$ where $\zeta_3$ is a primitive cube root of unity and $d$ is a positive cube-free integer. Our work examines the behavior of the chain of lattice minima in the cubic field $\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt[3]{d})$ arising from the prime factorization of $d$ in relation to generators of ambiguous principal ideals. Specifically, we investigate the occurrence of generators of such ideals among the lattice minima and explain both the anticipated and unexpected outcomes based on the application of Dirichlet's theorem on primitive roots.

A research framework is introduced to uncover and analyze decision-making processes of neural networks through the combination of expert-guided variables and layer-wise relevance analysis. Building on previous findings, it has been observed that networks trained with expert variables tend to replicate the conclusions drawn by experts. Furthermore, connecting network layers with relevant external variables allows for a deeper understanding of the network's internal structure and the features that are most influential in its decision-making process. This insight has proven useful in tagging jets at hadron colliders, specifically in distinguishing jet jets originating from jets of particles.

For every positive integer r, a specific kind of Stirling number is used to count how many ways a set can be divided into a specified number of non-empty subsets, where each subset contains at least r elements. We're introducing a variation of these Stirling numbers, which represents their extreme forms, reducing to well-known cases when r equals one. This paper seeks to establish formulas linking these variations together.

Eighty sets of layer groups were examined, each consisting of four types: ordinary and double, as well as gray single and double. Layer group properties allowed for the efficient computation of relevant physical characteristics using symbolic methods, thanks to code such as POLSym. This involved an initial step of categorizing irreducible domains based on their action within the Brillouin zone and the topology of the torus. Additionally, band representations stemming from site symmetry groups were broken down into irreducible components. This theoretical analysis was complemented by numerical checks, including the verification of Euler-Chern class formulas and the utilization of module theory.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators on a curved manifold, the use of coordinates adapted to the vector field's flow is inevitable. For fields with manifolds of codimension 1, this adaptation can result, effectively, in the generation of the coordinate system. The case for codimension 2 leads to a distinction. When attempting to generalize the Killing vectors to momentum operators within the framework of general relativity, it turns out that such a generalization is not feasible as it would imply a restrictive form for the metric. This article also delves into historical context and discusses momentum operators in terms of symmetry generators.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight. Our novel approach employs a complex neural network to approximate the combined effect of the transformed path and Jacobian, thereby distributing the free energy cost. By doing so, we achieve a substantial reduction in simulation variance. While our method specifically focuses on the Hubbard model, its principles can be extended to other systems suffering from sign problems.

In a composite Higgs model, we introduce doublet and triplet flavons with specific transformations under SU(2)L x U(1Y) to utilize non-holomorphic Yukawa couplings for generating fermion masses. We generate masses for all SM particles at the common scale of SU(4)C, where we also implement a mechanism to suppress the flavon vacuum expectation value to meet precise flavor oscillation constraints, while the flavon's heavier partner obtains a large mass through the composite vector resonances. We offer a detailed flavor structure within this model and perform a flavor stability analysis at the scalar potential level, demonstrating that the model can correctly produce fermion flavors. We also analyze the model's predictions for Higgs boson couplings and its potential to explain the anomalous magnetic moment of the muon.

The use of Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations, like redirected walking and haptics, extends VR interaction beyond conventional physical limitations by exploiting the boundaries of human perception. Examples of VPPM include walking farther than visible, interacting with objects beyond their apparent size, and moving beyond the visible room's bounds. While research has extensively analyzed the benefits of VPPM, there's less understanding of their potential adverse effects. Initial studies on the potential harms of redirected walking and fake floors indicate users may experience disorientation, nausea, and a sense of imbalance. Further concerns arise from users' inability to distinguish manipulated VR from real life. Additional potential risks have not yet been thoroughly examined. To address this, the present study outlines and discusses 10 potential consequences of VPPM. A manipulation is deemed a manipulation if it intentionally alters a user's perception to achieve unseen benefits. In addition to studying their drawbacks, researchers should develop guidelines and best practices for conducting manipulation experiments and assess the generalizability of manipulation-induced effects. Furthermore, the principle of minimal harm suggests that technologies causing disorientation or real-world confusion should be minimized. Ultimately, the author proposes the ethics by design principle to design VR systems that prevent the occurrence of VPPM.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we integrate German and Korean into BigScience's large-scale, 1.3 billion parameter multilingual language model, initially trained on 13 languages. Our study focuses on key factors influencing model adaptability for new languages and weighs the computational expense against potential performance gains.

Binary star systems are believed to form from the breaking up of a single cloud core.
The overall framework of how these stars form can be traced back to a core's initial rotation,
which causes the core to flatten and affects the core's internal movements and the shape of the core.
This shape change directly influences how core masses form and can alter the core's properties in critical ways.
Specifically, the core's potential as a gravitational object is altered, which directly affects the core's formation mass in important ways.
Our study aims to investigate the core's core formation mass in detail,
taking into account various core properties and measurements across multiple runs.
These core formation mass values are plotted against core masses to identify trends and patterns.
Our analysis in detail, takes core total mass into account and the core formation mass values increase significantly when the core is more massive.
This increase in formation mass values is significant, nearly four times larger,
which directly affects the upper limit of mass ratio between stars in these systems.
This outcome directly affects mass balance between stars in these systems and is an important consideration for astronomers to understand.
The upper mass balance limit is determined by cloud core properties and is an important consideration for binary star formation.
Our study provides valuable insights into how this limit is set by cloud core properties and is an important consideration for binary star formation.

This research introduces the m-arcsinh Kernel ('m-ar-K') Fast Independent Component Analysis ('FastICA') approach for extracting features from data sets. Initially, a new kernel function with outlier-resistant arcsinh behavior is developed. Subsequently, this new kernel is utilized within FastICA to improve its outlier resistance. Last, "m-ar-K FastICA" is demonstrated on several data sets to show its feature extraction capabilities in comparison to 'FastICA' and the 'nuMAX' kernel-based FastICA. Additionally, the method's outlier resistance is tested using the 'noisy MNIST' data set. Overall, 'm-ar-K FastICA' achieves comparable feature extraction performance to 'FastICA' and 'nuMAX kernel FastICA', while exhibiting superior outlier resistance.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory to algebraic and propositional proof systems. It's proven that if a logic can identify a specific polynomial-size family of graphs using an $o(\log n)$-sized formula, then the Extended Polynomial Calculus is also able to refute formulas within that same complexity range. Furthermore, it's established that the weak counting calculus, specifically #P(n)count, is included in the Extended Polynomial Calculus. Another finding is that the bounded variable calculus can be characterized by a specific polynomial-sized formula distinctiveness within the EPCC.

A subring collection is deemed $\sigma$-elementary if it encompasses all subrings of any ring within the family, which requires a finite number of ring subrings to define the entire collection's properties. It has been established that for each positive integer $\sigma$, there exists an infinite set of rings, each having a quotient field characteristic of characteristic 0, and each contains exactly $\sigma$ subrings. Furthermore, there exists an infinite set of integral domains with exactly $\sigma$ ideals.

Many fields make assertions that cannot be thoroughly disproven, particularly when they concern social dynamics. It can be challenging to verify such claims due to a lack of structured research and rigorous verification. There is often an overwhelming number of such claims, described in an unstructured manner, with varying levels of quality. As a result, high-quality claims may go overlooked in favor of inferior ones. A significant issue arises from these claims because they can be subject to misinterpretation, with people selectively extracting fragments and disseminating them, while also failing to address the full context. In response, we introduce a framework called PubMed which aims to address these challenges, and demonstrate its effectiveness through a series of experiments involving real-world application and a demonstration of its ability to structure complex social data through the analysis of a large corpus of online discussions.

Identifying trending social media events in real-time across various geographical locations is crucial, yet complex, due to the vast amount of concurrent social media content. Existing solutions either fail to detect rare events or struggle with real-time processing on diverse devices. This research presents a novel deep learning approach that accurately real-time localizes events in different regions and recognizes them within social media streams, simultaneously revealing hidden patterns in data. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through extensive experiments on multiple event datasets, both synthesized and from Twitter, outperforming other detection methods in various processing time frames. Synthetic data is available for research purposes at https://github.com/aman8901/SETEN.

New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background and galaxy surveys will enhance our understanding of the universe's development. However, this enhanced knowledge demands efficient analysis methods, such as the analysis of B-mode maps to detect non-Gaussian patterns. A major obstacle in this process is the significant data volume, resulting in extremely large file sizes for two-point correlations and three-dimensional data cubes for all-line-of-sight analyses. This problem restricts the feasibility of future surveys, such as CMB-S4, due to the necessary memory for handling the data. A solution to this issue is needed, such as FastSkew, which uses memory for calculating the B-mode map BISPECTRUM Estimator (FAST-BES) estimator. FastSkew applies data segmentation and pre-computation techniques to reduce the required memory for the analysis, enabling it to be performed on smaller memory systems.

By integrating Bayesian learning into adversarial training, a two-pronged approach to certifiable adversarial robustness is achieved. A recent study introduces a modified decision boundary, derived from the principles of adaptive robust generalization, which enables the development of certifiable approaches. Through a circular relationship between the Bayesian approach and this theory, four novel Bayesian algorithms are introduced. These methods draw on flexible family models and correlation-robust statistics. With the help of modern optimization techniques and hardware advancements, the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms is significantly improved. Furthermore, they exhibit superior performance on complex tasks such as image classification compared to existing standards. This body of research contributes to the broader understanding of adversarial robust learning through its connection to established concepts in adaptive statistics.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a machine learning method to identify the root cause of rumors. In this study, we analyzed the distribution patterns of top ten most prevalent rumors across various Chinese social media platforms from January to February 2020. We observed that these rumors predominantly adhered to a power-law pattern and a log-normal distribution. Furthermore, these outcomes validated the finite-type branching process model often applied to explain rumor propagation. Additionally, we found that pre-trained semantic network analysis could effectively pinpoint the primary source of rumors and constructed influence metrics based on this approach. These metrics enabled us to ascertain the top ten most influential accounts disseminating the top ten most prevalent rumors. Notably, these accounts primarily propagated politically motivated rumors.

This study investigates the impact of hyperspectral pixel dimensionality reduction on classification tasks. Various methods are used to reduce dimensions from 302 down to 2, employing both deterministic and stochastic methods such as PCA, LDA, and SNE. The primary objective is to assess the dimensionality reduction technique that preserves the most spectral information. Our analysis reveals that both PCA and LDA produce similar results when reducing dimensions, and both outperform SNE in maintaining spectral detail.

Neural networks are highly effective at solving complex tasks, but they often require significant computational resources to operate. The memory-intensive nature of these models can be a major limitation, especially when dealing with large datasets. To overcome this issue, researchers are focusing on model compression techniques for deep neural networks, which are critical for training, testing, and deploying these models efficiently. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the most recent advancements in neural network compression, covering an broad range of methods and scenarios. The discussion is structured around the fundamental operations within natural language processing models such as embeddings, linear layers, and non-linear activations. The paper aims to present existing approaches, evaluate their performance based on empirical results, and provide insights into future research directions.

A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and accurate calculation of crucial chemical shift values for proteins. ProCS predicts the pKa values and assigns chemical shifts to nearly all atoms in an unstructured protein in under a minute. The tool's output matches experimental data with a correlation coefficient of 0.92, allowing for accurate validation of proteins with correct folding. Experimentally determined and ProCS-calculated chemical shifts are compared, and their deviations from ideal values are analyzed. This analysis highlights the tool's ability to accurately calculate the hydrogen-bonding effects and side-chain influence on proteins. In addition, the tool's ability to model ions and water molecules in the solvent has been demonstrated, and its results align with molecular dynamics simulations. Finally, ProCS was used to find the most stable structure of a protein and compare it with experimental data.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a crucial decision. Despite initial assumptions that all standard loss functions are equivalent when calculating gradient steps, research has shown that this notion is flawed. Consequently, the effective impact of the loss function on a neural network's final performance is considerably larger than anticipated. This study delves into how the final neural network's performance is influenced by the selection of a loss function. Specifically, the investigation focuses on classifiers trained on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Notably, the analysis shows that certain loss functions are capable of utilizing all available data, including unlabeled images, enhancing the classifiers' accuracy. In this context, utilizing the unsupervised dataset comprises approximately 70% of the labeled data.

Describing the behavior of strongly correlated systems presents a significant challenge to theorists. As a response to this challenge, the parquet theory was introduced as a diagrammatic approach aimed at accurately capturing system behavior, despite this theory being challenging to implement due to the large number of diagrams involved and difficulties in generating them automatically. In an effort to simplify the theoretical framework, we formulate the parquet theory within a Hamiltonian formalism, using the many-body Hamiltonian theory as a starting point. Within this framework, parquet amplitudes are redefined as a transformation from the Hamiltonian amplitudes to a new set of components, and a simplified parquet equation is derived that expresses the Hamiltonian amplitudes as a function of these transformed components, with the hope that this equation can be efficiently solved using current diagrammatic techniques. Furthermore, we demonstrate the feasibility of solving the equation using a perturbation approach.

The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical phenomenon has been studied extensively but its observation experimentally remains an unresolved issue due to the limited sensitivity of existing measurement techniques. To overcome these obstacles, we have developed a method combining quantum chemical calculations and statistical physics to evaluate the degree of exciton coherence. By applying this approach to the material TiSe2, our findings reveal the presence of significant excitonic fluctuations, but no clear signs of exciton coherence phase transition even at the lowest temperatures. This research provides a foundation for further experimental investigation of this research topic.

In the US, various safety organizations have adopted text-based systems for processing community members' incident reports, which necessitated a closer look at interactions between community members and dispatchers through these platforms. To investigate, researchers analyzed the system logs of LiveSafe, a community safety tool, by creating a large dataset of over 50,000 incident reports and corresponding conversations between users and dispatchers. This dataset enabled researchers to investigate the underlying dynamics of community safety interactions, resulting in several key findings. Firstly, researchers observed significant differences in dispatcher training and its impact on the effectiveness of conversations. Secondly, the analysis revealed that dispatchers tend to ask more questions and provide less reassurance compared to the reverse. Lastly, various factors were found to contribute to the complexity of these conversations.

To analyze the impact of external magnetic fields on triplized triplized metals, researchers create a theoretical model based on a triplized nematic superconductor. They achieve this by using a simple yet accurate Hamiltonian that incorporates the appropriate magnetic interactions. By applying the Bogoliubov-de Gennes method, they obtain the ground state of the system under both the superconducting and paramagnetic states. Subsequently, they calculate the quantum oscillation frequencies for various magnetic field orientations. Their findings indicate that a characteristic triplized magnet exhibits specific patterns in its frequency responses that can be mapped onto a Fermi surface, with a particularly distinct frequency, [extract_itex]\Omega_{\textrm{min}}$, exhibiting a particularly distinct pattern of variation based on the electron interaction strength, [extract_itex]I_s[/extract_itex].

Label-efficient active learning algorithms query specific, representative samples to be annotated by a human. However, when human labelers have diverse backgrounds, their variations can negatively impact the model's performance. To address this challenge, we introduce a new minimax active learning framework for semi-supervised training and optimization, which takes into account human labeler diversity - MinAL. MinAL is an iterative process that alternates between selecting the most informative unlabeled data points and simulating different human labelers to maximize label diversity. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of MinAL in achieving a balance between model performance and label diversity, outperforming existing methods in both aspects. Code is available online at: https://github.com/criscianoj/minAL

To study how music changed over time from the year 1960 to 2010, we analyzed two types of complexity using information theory in the context of a genre-free analysis of Western music. The first type, temporal complexity, measures how much a song changes over time, while compositional complexity focuses on how much individual elements like melodies or harmonies stand out from each other. These complexities were calculated by examining two large collections of songs. Our analysis shows that temporal complexity evolves differently than what scientists previously predicted. Surprisingly, songs in both collections show increased time-based complexity over time, although their behaviors diverge when looking at the relationship between time and composition. When focusing on the amount of information in the songs, we found that this complexity follows a pattern over time, although the pattern isn't the same as the previous scientific prediction.

A novel classification system, derived from the theory of analytic combinatorics, is examined in this paper. It represents an analytical framework for understanding complex classification methods, focusing on multiple-entry processes with reinforcement. The study provides a generative model interpretation of this classification system, linking it to a theory of probabilistic analysis that offers precise predictions of its asymptotic behavior. By establishing connections within the analytic combinatorics field, the study determines the growth rate patterns of its constituent functions through the use of difference equations. Ultimately, the study applies a De Moivre-Dirichlet theorem to establish asymptotic results, the structure of which may also be relevant to the analysis of self-organizing universal coding methods.

Prawitz identified a key feature of Gentzen's intuitionistic natural deduction as the inversion principle, typically paired in proof-theoretic literature with the recovery principle. This paper presents an alternative, by reformulating both principles into a single requirement, referred to as the harmony condition, within the context of the Computational Ludics framework. This new framework illuminates the underlying notions: that the inversion principle embodies containment, while the recovery principle serves as its converse. Additionally, this paper derives and demonstrates the equivalence of the harmony condition with two further conditions defined in the Computational Ludics framework.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose grouping multiple comparisons together and allowing human labelers to efficiently identify clusters of tasks that are mutually comparable. We propose two approaches for this aggregation: one involves human labelers visually inspecting cluster members and marking comparable pairs, while the other relies on visual objects within cluster members to facilitate comparative analysis. We estimate the time savings from this aggregation and demonstrate the effectiveness of our solution through empirical results, showing that our approach using visual cues significantly cuts comparison time by over 80%.

We show that a topological space's Smyth powerspace is core-compact if and only if the original space has local compactness. Consequently, this implies the Smyth powerspace does not uniformly preserve core-compact properties.

We're investigating singular vorticities in ideal two-dimensional fluids with specific properties derived from point vortices and vortex sheets. These characteristics are represented by measure that conforms to conservation of active mass and momentum. In the absence of convexity, such vorticities become unstable under any conditions. However, in the presence of convexity, only specific vorticities remain stable without any external forces acting upon them. The analysis also extends to the effects of external forces acting along a specific direction. With a convexity present, only a limited set of forces leads to stationary solutions. The study involves a combination of functional analysis, specific constraints, and the application of the Hamiltonian principle.

The Average Treatment Effect (ATE) is a crucial concept in causal inference that measures the impact of a treatment.  In complex data environments with multiple confounders, the inverse probability weighting (IPW) method has become the go-to approach for estimating ATE.  However, inaccurate assumptions about these confounders can result in unreliable findings.  To address this issue, recent research introduced the normalized IPW (nIPW) method, which incorporates an additional parameter to counteract estimation inaccuracies.  While the nIPW method has shown substantial improvements, it relies on the propensity score to determine treatment assignment.  In scenarios where two treatments have similar probabilities, the propensity score may fail to capture all available information, and the nIPW method may still struggle.  To address this limitation, the proposed approach combines nIPW with neural network (NN) predictions.  Given access to additional feature information, the predictions can serve as supplementary variables for constructing an improved propensity score. The resulting method involves two steps: first, using NNs to estimate treatment probabilities based on this extended feature space, and second, recalibrating these estimates. The resulting estimates allow for more accurate ATE estimation. Compared to the nIPW method and IPW combined with loss minimization, the proposed method performed better in the author's simulation and real-world data analysis.

The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in lepton physics research.  
Recent data from LHC, Tevatron and SLAC's Belle II, ATLAS, CMS, D0 and Fermilab's TB08 collaborations have brought about a shift in the field, with new insights into $\tau$'s properties.  
A major task for theoretical researchers involves distinguishing between Standard Model and non-standard model effects.  
The complexity of $\tau$ is compounded by its several decay modes, each with its own set of challenges.  
In contrast to muon and muon-like leptons, whose interaction patterns are well understood, the $\tau$'s properties remain more enigmatic.  
To tackle this, precision measurements are critical, with theory needing to provide theoretical models that can withstand the tests of experimental data.  
A key aspect of this research is separating out non-standard models from the effects of quantum corrections.  
To facilitate this, lattice QCD is being used to calculate tau polarization, with new results being published by the FLACK and FSS groups.  
By comparing these results with data from LHC, ATLAS, D0, CMS, FERMILAB, TB08, SLAC's TB08, SLAC's SLAC and FERMILAB's FERMILAB experiments, researchers can pinpoint discrepancies between observed patterns and those predicted by non-standard models.

A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to cyclogenesis, namely the influence of rotation and temperature variations, by utilizing a unique setup that facilitates straightforward generation of a stable temperature gradient and rotation similar to the Coriolis effect, all within seconds to minutes. The experimental setup enables the creation of a baroclinic wave and allows for the observation of various aspects of wave behavior including momentum, vorticity, and temperature patterns. In addition, two techniques, thermochromic liquid crystals and schlieren optical breakdown flow visualization, have been used to visualize both the interfacial movement and air circulation within the setup. A numerical simulation based on the Navier-Stokes equations has been employed to further analyze the results and compare the experimental and simulated data through direct visualization of velocity, vorticity, and temperature patterns, showcasing excellent agreement including temporal variations of waves.

A typical strategy for modelling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process, using a threshold-dependent intensity model.  We suggest reparameterising this process in terms of the conditional probability of exceeding gradually increasing thresholds, which can be directly estimated from data and then used to model the underlying dependence on the exceedance probability.  We examine a number of threshold intensity models that are commonly used in practice, which involve both a constant and a time-varying parameter, and demonstrate how their suitable reparameterisations enable the development of flexible models that can be effectively fitted using standard Bayesian methods that are unlikely to have significant computational issues.  These models involve time, which is defined as the inter-arrival times of the exceedances, which are now expressed as random variables whose distribution depends on the threshold exceedance probabilities.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, we focus on adversarial robustness, a critical consideration in RL that ensures an policy's performance doesn't significantly decrease when subjected to slight data perturbations. Our work is set within a deterministic setting and is constrained by bounded corruption, limiting the amount of manipulated data below a specific threshold. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel bound on the policy value loss in robust offline RL, which is related to the concept of k-corroboration. This involves finding subsets of states where there exists at least a certain proportion of nearby states within their support. To achieve the proposed bound, we design an efficient and simple modified policy optimization algorithm, an adaptation of Belle. Our theoretical analysis also comes with associated costs, including a factor of log(P/D) and sqrt(K*P/D), representing the price for robustness.

This study demonstrates the implementation of the logarithmic convexity method within the context of the 1-D heat equation, specifically focusing on its utility in addressing the terminal strong approximate controllability issue in systems subject to impulsive controls and dynamic boundaries, thereby also resolving an extended version of the observability problem. Furthermore, it identifies and examines the significance of a crucial parameter λ in the system. If λ exceeds or equals the first eigenvalue of the 1-D Laplacian operator, the system with the boundary condition f(t,x)|B = 0 remains strongly approximatly controllable for all t > τ and initial conditions; when λ is less than the eigenvalue, the same level of controllability is achieved within a narrower time frame, specifically when t, τ, and the system's spatial dimension interact in a particular way.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of two major detection methods - model calibration and density estimation - in response to background and semantic shifts in data, which were found across various language understanding datasets. In our evaluation, density estimation outperformed model calibration in background shift scenarios but struggled with semantic shifts. We discovered that no single detection method excelled in handling all kinds of text distributions, so we proposed a new ensemble method that combines multiple techniques and showed it has improved overall performance.

In recent years, nanoscale devices have been designed that can mimic biological processes and mimic the movement of cellular components. These devices, known as brownian motors, use the random motion of particles to drive their operation. Researchers are currently developing advanced quantum devices, such as electron tunneling systems, to drive these motors. Studies have shown that quantum processes can generate and transfer energy, leading to the development of new technologies that combine quantum mechanics with the movement of particles. A simple model has been created to study quantum tunneling forces, finding that quantum mechanics can exert measurable forces that differ from those predicted by classical mechanics.

Building on a 2014 framework, researchers introduced various interpretations of transducer behavior, some differing significantly from traditional understandings. In this study, further insights into close approximations between two-way and one-way transducer models were gained. Specifically, we introduce the notion of one-way resynchronizability, a requirement for two-way transducers to be closely approximated by one-way models in terms of output length. This concept aligns with one-way soundness for one way unbounded soundness. By redefining soundness in a more relevant context, we show that one-way resynchronizability等同于 two-way one-way soundness. This equivalence leads to a new result: the classes of languages accepted by one-way acceptors and two-way balanced acceptors are equivalent. However, this equivalence does not hold for one-way strictly sound two-way acceptors. Distinguishing between weakly and strictly sound two-way transducers remains an unresolved issue in this field.

This note introduces an efficient algorithm for quickly determining the coefficients of the product of two polynomials, given their coefficients. For a polynomial with n terms, the algorithm finds the coefficients of the ensuing polynomial with approximately 1.285n terms. This process can be accomplished with a computational complexity of O(n log n), which is a significant improvement in efficiency. Crucially, the algorithm operates offline and is space-efficient, requiring only a constant amount of additional memory. By leveraging any existing fast Fourier transform, the algorithm produces the result. This algorithm builds upon the foundation of a earlier study by J. Buk and V. Rodl, who showed that specific convolution sequences can be generated from shorter sequences. This development allows for faster computation in specific scenarios, with practical applications in deriving closed-form expressions for combinatorial sequences.

To search for the potential existence of the unique $0^{--}$ state, a transition from the well-known $1^{--}$ state $Y(4630)$ to the charmonium $0^{++}$ state $\eta_{c}(2984)$ is examined. Based on QCD sum rules, the difference in interference between these two states is calculated, yielding the decay width of $Y(4630)$ to $\eta_{c}(2984)$ and providing an expectation for this process to be detectable. Furthermore, an analysis of possible decay channels of $Y(4630)$ to a photon and either $\eta$ or $\eta'$ states suggests the latter is the more feasible option. Ultimately, it is proposed that the $Y(4630)$ decay to $\eta_{c}(2984)$ and a photon is the most promising discovery strategy, with a recommendation for verification at BESIII using a specific selection criterion.

A crucial prediction of the Standard Model is tested with the joint measurement of the phase $\phi_s$ and decay width difference $\Delta\Gamma_s$ in $s$ quark decay processes. Initially, the data were found to be inconsistent with the Standard Model expectation due to large uncertainties. Recent updates to the analysis, incorporating the resonance search in the $K_K^*$ system, have reduced the discrepancy and made it appear consistent with the Standard Model prediction. Further analyses are underway to ultimately confirm the existence of new physics beyond the current theoretical frameworks.

Airborne transmission of respiratory diseases like COVID-19 is a significant concern, with public transport settings like buses being of particular worry. Understanding how long an infected person can transmit the virus, how far it travels, and the effectiveness of ventilation in neutralizing the virus on a bus are crucial. These factors vary greatly due to differences in seating arrangements, ventilation systems, and individual passenger movements. Developing precise computational models that simulate these dynamics is complex and costly. In contrast, the quasihomogeneous or 'well-mixed' model, although simpler and faster to use, has not been fully utilized to facilitate design optimizations for public transport settings. This research assesses the well-mixed model's utility in evaluating the parameters that influence disease spread, travel distance of the virus, and virus neutralization in an urban bus environment. By comparing the well-mixed model's predictions with those of a high-fidelity Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) model under normal and high ventilation conditions, the study evaluates the well-mixed model's effectiveness in optimizing public transport settings to minimize the risk of respiratory disease transmission.

This study has conducted large-scale shell-model computations for $\beta$-decay attributes. Researchers have performed similar calculations for $\beta$-decay properties. Furthermore, it has involved calculating single electron capture quantities by adapting shell-model operators and inputs. Data on $^{133}$Te $\beta$-decay properties were collected and compared. In addition, theoretical results for the capture properties of $^{137}$Te have been computed. Finally, the work on tellurium's relevant characteristics is set to contribute towards improving experimental investigations on isotopes using CRENATe at ISOLDE/CERN.

Double-sided auctions are commonly used in financial markets to facilitate the matching of demand and supply. Our work builds on prior research, which significantly reduced complexity in algorithmic auction implementation, and further advances this field. A key innovation is the ability to support a wider range of auction features. This includes not only complex order types but also the verification of established auction rules. Specifically, we focus on German stock exchanges in Europe, which have distinct rules and order types. Our methodology relies on verified software, where we list all matching rules in formal language and algorithmically verify their correctness against established rules. The resulting algorithm is then verified to ensure it is bug-free. Using this approach, we achieved verification on actual exchange data, with no discrepancies found. This confirms that the algorithm is effective in handling real-world scenarios and scenarios not present in the simulation.

We utilized heavy quark effective theory to investigate the $F$-wave bottom mesons, applying both theoretical and experimental data to calculate the mass of these mesons. Additionally, by examining the decay widths of bottom mesons, we derived upper limits on their corresponding coupling values. Our research further included constructing Regge trajectories in the planes of angular momentum (J) and squared mass (M^2), yielding predictions that align neatly with Regge theory lines. These outcomes may hold significant implications for future experimental research on this topic.

Michal Szabados initially proposed a theory in his doctoral dissertation. In this current paper, the proposed conjecture is examined by the authors, specifically a Ph.D. hypothesis by Michal Szabados. Initially, the researchers demonstrate that an evaluation could be narrowed down to a periodic structure, defined over a specific and limited character set. It is further established that Szabados's conjecture is true for a considerable class of non-regular patterns. This includes all low-convex patterns of relatively simple complexity.

In the field of nonlinear science, extracting meaningful patterns from large datasets is a crucial task. Low-rank matrix decomposition is one approach used for this purpose. Dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) is a type of low-rank matrix decomposition that focuses on discovering the underlying dynamics in data, particularly how one variable influences another. However, traditional DMD has limitations in accurately modeling complex systems, especially those with data correlations close to unity. This can result in the failure of DMD to correctly describe the system's evolution, a problem known as eigenvalue ambiguation. To address this, researchers have developed a new algorithm called Kernel LANDO that uses a kernel trick to overcome this limitation. This method employs a maximum likelihood estimation approach in a linear kernel space, allowing it to accurately compute DMD-like eigenvalues and vectors that describe the system's evolution with near unity norms. This method is highly efficient and can be applied to datasets of varying sizes without suffering from ambient curvature.

The online chess community has formed massive, intricate networks of associations through the shared knowledge of chess openings. The prevalence of specific opening sequences is a sign of a deeper, collective understanding, with researchers extracting statistical insights from The Chess Vantage Database. Specific findings reveal a strong relationship between frequency and chess opening complexity, with most chess sequences belonging to a minority category, whereas elite players tend to focus on more intricate and frequently observed openings. Also, enhancements to the Chess Vantage Database enable the measurement of similarity between frequency-based chess openings, which are often linked and demonstrate a gradual shift from unfamiliar to sophisticated sequences.

This research explores the observational characteristics of millisecond pulsars in terms of their magnetic fields, rotational periods, and masses. Our analysis is grounded in the concept of accretion-induced collapse of white dwarfs within binary star systems, enabling a more nuanced comprehension of millisecond pulsar demographics. Moreover, our findings underscore the significant evolutionary linkage between neutron stars and white dwarfs within stellar binary systems, particularly through the process of accretion-induced collapse.

A method to derive constants of motion beyond local bounds for ODE-based Lagrangian systems is outlined, including a practical example that illustrates its utility for dissipative mechanical systems and its implications on solution existence and behavior under specific assumptions. The framework is further extended to cover Euler-Lagrange equations with order greater than two, yielding new first integrals for particular models, such as the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator, paving the way for potential applications in Euler-Lagrange partial differential equations in the future.

Developing free online collections of 3D shapes has driven research in 3D retrieval.  However, most datasets are limited to 2D images since capturing labeled 3D data is time-consuming.  Shape retrieval from a single 2D image or a freehand sketch is still challenging due to 2D to 3D translation ambiguity.  In the fields of computer vision and graphics, sketching has gained attention for its ability to capture human concepts and creativity.  While sketching is commonly used in 2D, its potential in creating and describing 3D objects in virtual reality is yet to be fully explored.  This paper will investigate how to leverage retrieved information from 2D VR sketches to reconstruct the original object, and also how to effectively perform shape retrieval with such sketches.

HD80606b, a planet discovered in its host star's vicinity, undergoes a notable 1-month journey around its orbit that lasts only six days near its closest approach.  Its unique trajectory provides valuable insights into the atmosphere and other characteristics of eccentric planets when combined with spectroscopy during different phases of its orbit.  Because of its complex orbit, further observations are necessary for HD80606b to take full advantage of the capabilities of the James Webb Space Telescope.  Researchers used data from various space and ground-based observatories along with algorithms to transfer orbital information and refine the timing of HD80606b's closest approach.  They then simulated the orbital path the planet would follow if its orbit had not been adjusted, discovering that the transmission of light received by the sky-based telescopes remains the same, but significant differences are observed in the light received by the ground-based telescopes.  As a result, the unadjusted orbit predicts that the planet transits its host star 3.5 days later than anticipated.  By taking advantage of the light received by the space and ground-based telescopes and incorporating the uncertainties in the measurements, researchers have created a refined model that accurately represents the trajectory of HD80606b. In this investigation, we delve into the possibility of isentropic collapse for a perfect fluid employing a variety of equations of state, particularly focusing on the type $p = \alpha \rho$ or $p = \alpha T$. We find that if the dependence on density alone, with a non-negative coefficient $\alpha$, is considered, isentropic conditions result in a lack of a singularity or end to collapse. Conversely, if the pressure's dependence on temperature, with a non-negative coefficient $\alpha$, is assumed, we observe that under certain circumstances, specifically when the parameter $\alpha$ is small and satisfies the condition $\alpha \leq \frac{2}{3\pi} \sqrt{1-\frac{2m}{r}}$, a singularity or end to collapse does occur.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we have developed a comprehensive method for deriving corrections to the extremality bounds of arbitrary four-dimensional black holes. Our approach involves introducing systematic perturbations to the mass and entropy of an extremal black hole. Consequently, a cornerstone theorem in black hole physics has been established, enabling the calculation of higher-order corrections to various properties, such as mass, entropy, and electric charge. Furthermore, several examples have been analyzed using this framework, including the Kerr-Newman black hole, a pair of coincident extremal Kerr-Newman rings, and a family of four-dimensional supergravity solutions.

A key goal in robotic learning is to develop effective robotic policies.
There's substantial research on robotic policy learning that draws from the
field of reinforcement learning. However, current approaches to learning
end-effector tasks often involve joint control, making them difficult to
implement. Furthermore, these policies are typically evaluated in a static
environment, neglecting the impact of external forces and disturbances.
This paper presents an exploration drive designed to facilitate learning in
end-effectors during interactive tasks. Initially, we identify a challenge:
exploratory movements learned by end-effecters may not necessarily be useful.
Next, we propose integrating this drive with model-based planners to ensure
that the learning process remains efficient. Additionally, we introduce a
method for transferring skills from a virtual environment to the robot through
teleoperation. Finally, we test our approach on a variety of tasks, including a
dynamically adjustable tabletop and a fetching task executed in teleoperation.

A generalized three-dimensional Poincaré algebra has been developed that incorporates colour symmetry. This enhanced algebra can serve as a basis for modelling coloured Poincaré gravity and exploring generalised models of massive and massless free particles in three dimensions. Multiple generalised particle models have been presented, which distinguish themselves in terms of the coloured Poincaré orbits they describe. Our methodology provides a potential pathway to describing particles in non-abelian backgrounds and serves as a starting point for the worldline formulation of an associated quantum field theory.

We have devised three new parameterized algorithms for identifying whether a directed graph can be represented in an upward planar layout. Specifically, we've developed a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the number of source vertices, an XP algorithm based on the graph's treewidth, and a fixed-parameter algorithm based on the treedepth parameter. Our novel method combines parameterized techniques with SPQR tree-decompositions, extending previous tractability findings on series-parallel graphs, single-source graphs, and outerplanar graphs.

Image-based visual navigation using external memories has shown promise in handling real-world complexities, but its potential is not fully realized due to the common approach of selecting memories based on simple, local criteria. We propose MemoNav, a novel method that overcomes this limitation. MemoNav dynamically chooses the most informative memories from a whole database through adaptive mini-batching during training. This results in a navigation agent that relies on selective memories for improved real-world performance compared to agents using full-database training. Additionally, we develop MemoeEgo, an open-source dataset and benchmark that promotes research into memory-based navigation, along with a detailed analysis offering guidance for future research in this area. Our MemoNav implementation is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ailab-albert/SRLab_Code_MemoNav/tree/main.

To increase cellular capacity, operators initially implemented 4G LTE small cells with lower transmission powers. However, as they failed to meet demand for ultra-high data rates in the post-COVID era, operators began deploying 5G small cells. This study compares low, medium, and high power 4G/5G/6G small cells in terms of their effects on network coverage and backhaul requirements. It proposes that 6G small cells will need lower power levels than currently seen in 5G, while their increased processing capabilities will allow for more efficient use of pipe-based backhaul. Ultimately, this could lead to a future where even rural areas have access to high-speed internet.

We've developed a comprehensive framework to model complex interactions between multiple entangled systems using hypergraphs. This approach can be applied to several processes and we'll specifically explore how certain conditions lead to spontaneous pattern emergence in systems that follow the Rock-Paper-Scissors dynamics.

This study examines the operator growth phenomenon in Lie-symmetric systems by utilizing concepts from quantum information theory. We specifically analyze Krylov complexity, entanglement properties, and information capacity within SU(1,1) and SU(2) symmetric systems, leveraging two-mode coherent states as a primary tool. These coherent states enable us to explore operator growth patterns and entanglement structures in a wide range of scenarios, ultimately verifying that certain features are inherent to systems with Lie symmetry. Additionally, we investigate the impact of disorder on operator growth and entanglement, considering both SU(1,1) and SU(2) cases. Our work is set within the context of a non-autonomous SU(1,1) system and an ergodic disorder model based on the Heisenberg dual-harmonic oscillator.

The atomic structure of the Hoyle state, a state of extreme carbon abundance in the universe, is crucial to understanding the carbon availability for the universe's composition. Theoretical models of the Hoyle state's wave function are being tested to understand its behavior and the fluctuations it experiences. The non-relativistic effective theory of the nucleus is used to model the dynamics of the Holetrie state and the carbon nucleus. The carbon-12 ground state's medium-induced effective interaction is analyzed to understand its behavior. The theory is used to calculate the root mean square displacement of the Holetrie state's wave function. The outcomes of the calculation are being compared to the outcomes of the double-phi-p measurement done by the CERES/PHENIX collaboration. The data may be interpreted as the energy produced by the decay of the Holetrie state into two phi-particles and an excited carbon-12 ground state.

Significant breakthroughs in understanding and modeling dynamic fracture have been achieved with the development and implementation of coherent zone models. The coherence zone model incorporates two key factors - an intrinsic material length scale and an intrinsic time scale - to better capture dynamic fracture behavior. Through numerical simulations using the intrinsic coherence zone model, the influence of these two material intrinsic factors on the dynamics of a crack in a plate under dynamic fracture conditions was investigated. The results show that when the coherence zone model includes both material intrinsic length and time scales, an intrinsic time scale effect emerges, leading to oscillatory modes appearing at higher loading rates than when the model considers only the material intrinsic length scale, as in the phase field model. The model also accurately predicts the transition from a branching mode to a tip splitting mode, matching experimental observations where multiple cracks emerge simultaneously at a given threshold rate. Furthermore, a theoretical analysis was developed to predict the rate threshold at which tip splitting occurs, showing a strong correlation with experimentally determined rate thresholds for tip splitting.

In a general setting, we examine the properties of finite state channels equipped with feedback and state information, which becomes available to the encoder in a predictable sequence. This encompasses a broad range of channels, including memoryless channels with independent and identically distributed states (referred to as the Shannon strategy), channels with Markovian states that offer the ability to access past states (known as look-ahead access), and universal decoding machines subject to limited errors. Our study provides upper and lower bounds on the capacity of these channels by employing two distinct techniques: first, we derive a method to determine the maximum achievable rates via the development of "universal" codes; second, we present a method to determine the maximum rates via the analysis of joint typical sequences and projections. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our findings by determining the capacity look-ahead access channels for a two-state symmetric Markov chain and in the absence of look-ahead access, we establish a gap between the achievable rates and the maximum rates.

A novel class of superconductors with attractive spin-orbit coupling has been proposed, 
and we utilize the Ruckenstein-McMillan-Hubbard model to study their properties.
Theoretically, we find that the ground state of this model exhibits singlet characteristic, 
which leads to the emergence of topological superconductivity under specific conditions.
Numerically, we demonstrate that topological superconductivity is most robust when there is an optimal balance between monochromatic and checkerboard pairings.
The derived equation reveals that topological edge states arise due to a non-trivial bulk property, 
and we both theoretically and numerically investigate the influence of kinetic energy on these states.
The resulting calculations show that these edge states survive when the influence of kinetic energy is not overly intense, 
accompanied by the simultaneous occurrence of monochromatic and checkerboard order parameters.
The discovered phenomenon of topological edge states exhibits resilience against monochromatic and checkerboard order parameter fluctuations,
