Between 2018 and 2019, four $K$2 plates were utilized for the LAMOST Time-domain Survey's first results. These initial studies aimed to optimize the survey's methodology by conducting one full run on each plate. Consistent findings emerged across the four plates, each containing 4000 spectra, which were then subjected to a comprehensive analysis. This involved adept handling of varying signal-to-noise levels, effective detection of variable stars, and precise recognition of galactic spectra. Notably, the plates demonstrated robust resistance to systemic errors and successfully identified over 7000 variable stars within a broad magnitude range of $B_V \in [9,15]$. These discoveries will serve as a solid foundation for the LATS' development and will contribute significantly to its future goals.

Recent advancements in SRAM-based True Random Number Generators have led to a shift in exploration towards supply voltage underscaling to enhance performance and efficiency. Nevertheless, SRAM-based TRNGs employing voltage underscaling still face challenges related to reliability. In this paper, a method for constructing a reliable SRAM-based TRNG through voltage underscaling is presented. By leveraging the variability in SRAM cell initialization failures, an SRAM-based TRNG is designed that utilizes supply voltage underscaling to accelerate entropy source initialization via the fast write method. Additionally, to ensure reliability, a supply voltage monitor, entropy extractor, and enhancement of the entropy source using supply failure patterns are incorporated into the design. As a result, a dependable and efficient SRAM-based TRNG is achieved. Experimental validation using commercial 65nm SRAM cells has demonstrated that the proposed TRNG can offer a maximum throughput of 3MBPS with a reliability level surpassing $10^{-9}$ at a energy consumption rate less than $10^{-9}J/b$. Furthermore, a significant reduction in energy consumption by a factor of 4 and 30, along with increased performance and reliability by a factor of 2 and 5, are observed compared to state-of-the-art TRNG designs focusing on energy efficiency and reliability respectively.

A preliminary design and simulation of a single-electron resistive switch has been developed, incorporating two linear molecules that interact electrostatically: one molecule is a single-electron transistor and the other is a single-electron trap. To confirm the switch's functionality, circuit simulations have been conducted, which also verify its suitability for data storage by showing that electrical current can shift between two distinct states and that these states remain stable over time due to the molecules' inherent properties. Additionally, the design offers the potential for significantly higher density compared to conventional resistive switch technologies due to the minute size of single electrons and charges.

The concept of loop-tree duality has emerged as a promising approach for numerically computing complex multi-loop scattering amplitudes, offering an alternative to traditional methods. In the traditional approach, loop momentum integration is performed fully before calculating the scattering kernel based on external momenta. However, adopting loop momentum-driven numerical methods is impractical due to the non-trivial nature of the kernel. By delaying evaluation until the boundary of the phase space in multi-phase-space multi-loop cuts, the importance sampling in importance sampling is effectively aligned with the phase-space itself. As a result, efficient numerical methods can be employed, even in the presence of high-energy singularities. In our recent work, the loop momentum-driven strategy has been refined to include handling scalar spines in loop diagrams, which simplifies the scattering kernel. This simplification allows the use of traditional importance sampling methods with minimal modifications.

This paper aims to provide a direct and straightforward proof of a specific eigenfunction expansion formula for one-dimensional quantum walks with two possible states. A related formula was initially established using an indirect method via Herglotz-Nikishin function properties. Our approach involves expanding the eigenfunctions in terms of special functions known as Mouhot-Toscani functions and then deriving the required coefficients using a specific determinant formula.

This study examines the composition of hybrid stars formed by neutrons, protons, and various other particles. The analysis combines the Sigma-omega-rho model for a specific nuclear phase with two distinct quark phase models, and incorporates Maxwell and Gibbs conditions to understand the phase transition. By analyzing mass-radius relations, a hybrid star's mass is predicted to be limited to twice the mass of the sun.

The introduction of $q$-deformation into optomechanical systems reveals opportunities to explore and amplify non-linear effects. In this context, researchers have integrated a deformed Fabry-Perot cavity with a ring laser and a damped oscillator. It has been discovered that the $q$-deformation parameter significantly impacts the phase velocity of light within the system. Notably, specific values of this parameter can result in exceptional light slowing, fastening, reverse Cherenkov radiation, and even complete absorption of the probe beam under resonance conditions from the pump. Mathematical modeling, based on the $q$-deformed Hamiltonian, shows that the pump field influences the phase velocity and, consequently, allows control over the phase shift using the $q$-deformation parameter. In addition, the phase shift has been found to be contingent on both the probe and pump probe intensities. Furthermore, the minimum phase shift angle was observed to decrease as a function of probe intensity and to be influenced by both the decay rates of the oscillator and the optomechanical element. Moreover, researchers have explored the possibility of generating unsaturated optical transparency, as well as high levels of optical enhancement in this system. It has been observed that the amplitude susceptibility can be minimized and even adjusted to match a desired value by varying system parameters. Also, the system demonstrated the ability to amplify the probe signal when operated in the in-phase regime with in-phase pumping.

In a previous study, I developed a model where the Two-Rotors Model's negative scissors states, consisting of two-sided classical bodies, exhibited 1 |K| = 1; 0 components and negative space parity. Building on this work, I explored reflections in a plane that aligns with the rotors' symmetry axes, resulting in R-negative states with positive parity. Furthermore, I established a connection between reflections and R-operations, relating them to specific internal changes within the rotors, which I then used to calculate and compare the electromagnetic transition strengths of these states with those of their positive scissors mode counterparts.

The properties of thin films composed of oxules exhibit significant relevance both fundamentally and technologically. When specific ions within oxide thin films possess an odd number of electrons, they naturally generate a magnetic field. This study examines methods for creating advanced thin films, utilizing them as prototypes to investigate the behavior of magnetic subcomponents and explore innovative applications based on these unique properties.

The occurrence of diffusion, typically associated with stochastic processes, is ubiquitous in nature. In typical scenarios, random changes occur at a rate that aligns with the square root of time. In contrast, atoms in a laser-cooled setup exhibit a different behavior. In this research, we investigated the movement of a single, cooled atom within an optical lattice at equilibrium and discovered that its displacement grows linearly with the square root of time. However, at longer times, the atom's displacement grows as the time raised to the 0.75 power. The underlying cause of this movement can be attributed to a balance between the atom's damping from laser cooling and its thermal fluctuations, amplified by the optical lattice. As a result, traditional algorithms for estimating parameters are inefficient in this context. Instead, we propose and demonstrate the effectiveness of a new estimation method based on maximum likelihood estimation.

The trading interconnectedness between cryptocurrency assets is examined from the perspective of a network in this study, with the author investigating both pairwise correlations and broader patterns over a prolonged period. Data analysis focuses on daily price changes for 100 leading cryptocurrencies from January 2018 to March 2021, with the data then modeled using Markov Random Fields and Graphical Models. Multiple measures are employed to evaluate both linear and non-linear correlations, including a new correlation metric. Additionally, the influence of individual events and major market shifts on these correlations is investigated.

The formation of particles from trace gases is a crucial source of cloud condensation nuclei that facilitate the creation of clouds due to their role in overcoming extremely high supersaturation levels needed for pure water clusters to form. The precise chemical composition and structural characteristics of these initial particles are not yet clearly understood. The initial stages of this process involve the interaction of sulfuric acid with water, starting with the dimer of the two substances. The stabilization of this interaction requires the consideration of zero-point motion effects. Our research indicates that these effects significantly influence the dimer's stability, particularly in the region of the protonated species, where it eliminates the previously identified imaginary frequency in the two-substance interaction. The studies on the structures, properties, and conformational changes in the dimer were conducted in a zero-temperature environment, with the inclusion of zero-point motion effects through molecular dynamics simulations, where the simulations included an implicit consideration of these effects. The simulations included the analysis of the structures, proton positions, and the water sub-dimer's changes. Moreover, the calculations of the water sub-dimer's changes involved an analysis of the water sub-cluster frequency, where it was determined that the frequency changed from an imaginary to a real frequency, indicating that the zero-point motion effects significantly contribute to the dimer's stability.

We establish the definition of a compactification for a perception pair (X,Q), employing it to derive the definition of a quasisometry for such pairs. The developed framework results in the creation of a compact space, consisting of all group equivariant, bounded, non-expansive operators from X to its compactification. This operator space compactification generalises the original compactification of the metric space of bounded non-expansive operators over a metric space X discovered by Zhukov. Furthermore, our framework yields the discovery of novel operator-based compactifications, including one associated with the real line.

The way solids respond to temperature gradients can be understood by likening it to gravity's effect in space. In studying this, researchers focus on a key aspect known as the thermal Hall response. When investigating this, a significant finding emerges: an analogy between gravitational forces and temperature differences, often comparisons are made between external and internal forces. However, a crucial comparison has been missing until now: the analogy between mechanical stress and thermal energy accumulation. Through detailed mathematical analysis, this missing comparison is revealed, along with the discovery that Einstein relations hold true only under very specific conditions. These findings have important implications for understanding the physical properties of materials and their behavior under different environmental conditions.

In various machine learning scenarios, simpler models are generally preferred to their more complex counterparts, and controlling model complexity is a key function of regularizers. This study, drawing from classification tasks, examines how certain geometric properties of neural networks serve as a regularization mechanism, a finding supported by the observation that different neural architectures produce distinct solutions. The evidence suggests that the choice of neural network structure inherently acts as a regularizer, and this effect is largely overlooked in current research, which often attributes complexity control to the hyperparameters being tested.

A new approach for directly extracting the Wilson coefficients of rare $b\to s$ processes is developed using $B^0\to K^{*0}\mu^+\mu^-$ decays within an unbinned maximum likelihood framework. This novel method outperforms traditional Wilson coefficient determination by utilizing all available data and accounting for experimental correlations without segmentation into $q^2$ bins. Simulation results confirm the improved sensitivity and potential to leverage the complete Run 1 and 2 LHCb dataset in practice.

Automated essay grading has been a persistent challenge in Natural Language Processing.  Despite years of research, it remains an intricate task due to the diverse factors such as writing style, argument quality, and language nuances that make it difficult for machines to evaluate written essays compared to word-based problems.  This study delves into the efficacy of data augmentation methods employing Transformer models in enhancing the accuracy of essays scored by both traditional deep learning methods as well as the prominent state-of-the-art transformer models, specifically QNLI and BERT.

Given a simplicial complex defining a tensor's marginalizations, we restrict them to rank one, an idea developed from Kirkup and Sullivant's work on toric models. We delve into the toric ideals arising from such marginal independence models, with a specific focus on models for random graphs and matroids' independent set polytopes. We also explore numerical methods for parameter estimation through both Euclidean distance and maximum likelihood techniques and establish a database for small model examples.

A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model explores how distributing these opportunities impacts social mobility. By comparing predicted outcomes with real-world data, the model's findings indicate that the optimal method to maximize social mobility is to assign these opportunities randomly. However, the model also shows that a more equitable method—allocating these opportunities based on parental income within a specific range—can improve social mobility. Conversely, the most effective method to boost individual upmobility is to assign these opportunities to poorer families first and then distribute the remaining opportunities randomly.

The symmetry of wavefunctions under parity for particles of arbitrary spin is responsible for determining the wavefunction exchange statistics when the particles are permuted. According to non-relativistic quantum mechanics, the properties of angular momentum alone account for the sign factor resulting from the particle permutation, which relates spin to particle exchange statistics in this context.

We introduce an upgraded RingCT protocol that supports stealth addresses in conjunction with Delegated Proof of Stake, resulting in Delegated RingCT.
The Delegated RingCT scheme is comprised of an integrated signature and encryption framework, combining a public key encryption protocol and two types of signatures along with linkable ring signatures.
Our findings show that Delegated RingCT is feasible and can be seamlessly integrated into the Monero protocol.
Additionally, Delegated RingCT yields a substantial performance boost when compared to the original RingCT protocol.
Specifically, the transaction signing time for Delegated RingCT was found to be 2.5 to the power of n times swifter than RingCT, where n represents the number of input spending key pairs within a transaction.
Furthermore, the storage requirements for Delegated RingCT were observed to be significantly lower when compared to RingCT.
The computational requirements for verifying a Delegated RingCT transaction are minimal and involve just 250 millisecond checks, in contrast to the 1.3 second requirement for RingCT verification.

If more specific subclasses of linear systems can be solved in near-logarithmic space, this capability can be applied to solve a broader range of linear systems within a similar space complexity. Our findings build on work by Kyng and Zhang who previously made similar discoveries in terms of time complexity, utilizing reductions between approximate solvers; our own proof demonstrates that these reductions can be implemented using threshold circuits with specific characteristics.

Researchers have made the initial detection of three massive gauge bosons being produced simultaneously in collisions between protons at 13 TeV of energy.  This discovery stems from an examination of events involving highly charged leptons and substantial energy transfers, at the LHC with its 13 TeV of proton-proton center-of-mass energy.  The analysis focused on two distinct final states of heavy bosons, one consisting of a pair of same-flavored leptons and a second, differently charged lepton, paired with significant energy transfers.  Comparisons between predicted patterns of heavy boson creation and observed results were performed with the expectation of finding no discernible deviation from the standard model of particle physics.  Specifically, it was detected that the rates of heavy boson creation match predictions of standard model particle physics within estimated measurement uncertainties.  Furthermore, it was detected that limit conditions can restrict the mass sum of certain hypothetical particles by up to 2.5 TeV at the 95% confidence level.

Previous foundational Hebrew NLP tasks have heavily relied on the 30-year-old Hebrew Treebank. This outdated resource has likely limited previous achievements, so we propose a more current alternative. A second wave of UD-style labeling was conducted on "Neves Imladim," a modern Hebrew corpus, expanding the existing Hebrew NLP community. Our study involves evaluating and comparing state-of-the-art models for dependency parsing on various domains. The results show that while no single model excels in all settings, a combination of models performs best overall. Specifically, we observe that in the Hebrew NLP community, it is time to adopt and embrace new, modern techniques and move beyond the reliance on proven but outdated methods.

We demonstrate that any finite set in an $L_p$ space can be approximately reduced dimension while preserving its Euclidean distance, achieving a level of incompressibility. This level is defined by the minimum number of points required to form a subset, where the distance between any two points in the set is approximately equal to a fixed value, $\varepsilon$. Our result improves a previous bound by the Factorial function and approaches an optimal bound proposed by Kedlaya, Peled, and Volovikov, leaving a gap between the two bounds.

Recent breakthroughs in artificial neural networks have accelerated the growth of data-driven modeling in mechanics, making it possible to tackle complex problems in geotechnical engineering. Despite the success, a notable limitation of current approaches is their non-transferable nature, requiring an extensive retraining and large datasets whenever the problem setting changes. In response to this challenge, the concept of transfer learning was introduced to facilitate the sharing and application of existing knowledge across diverse problems. Building upon this idea, the present work delves into cooperative learning, where multiple agents learn and improve simultaneously through interaction and mutual benefit. Specifically, a new framework for the stable and efficient prediction of soil shear strength parameters, known as critical state soil mechanics, is developed using this cooperative approach. The proposed framework leverages a multi-agent deep neural network setup, where different agents model distinct variables (soil shear strength parameters) within the CSSTM framework, resulting in improved transfer and generalization capabilities, as demonstrated through validation against empirical data.

Current studies examining the performance of random low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes assume the presence of degree degree correlation in codes. However, based on empirical observations and simulations, we observe that actual transmitted LDPC codes exhibit this correlation. To better reflect these assumptions, we develop a correlated LDPC ensemble, then utilize both theoretical modeling and simulations to analyze its performance. Our analysis reveals that the correlated LDPC ensemble outperforms the traditional LDPC ensemble, particularly at low signal-to-noise ratios. To determine the optimal degree degree correlation, we develop an iterative procedure. Additionally, we discover that symmetric degree degree correlation provides the most effective improvement in performance while minimizing complexity.

An advanced modular system, which is known as the safety filter, has been designed to enhance the safety of autonomous systems like self-driving cars and robotic arms. This design, which is based on Model Predictive Control (MPC), ensures that any safety rules are always respected even when external disturbances occur. Although MPC offers excellent disturbance handling and performance, it has a significant shortcoming in that it cannot prevent infinite loops under certain types of disturbance. To address this issue, we have developed a new safety filter, which is based on SLS and ensures that the system remains safe despite the occurrence of unbounded disturbance. This innovative safety filter has been proven through rigorous mathematical analysis. The effectiveness of this new design has also been demonstrated through numerical examples.

A critical flaw exists in the current application of quantum key distribution (QKD) systems due to their vulnerability to quantum hacking. To address this, our team developed a novel and straightforward method that accurately replicates the Decoy-state QKD system's behavior but without strictly adhering to its parameters. By utilizing a limited range of discrete phase randomizations, our model efficiently achieves this purpose while keeping computational resources accessible. We validated the accuracy of our algorithm by comparing outcomes with standard Decoy-state QKD system predictions, demonstrating substantial consistency in both multi-photon probabilities and secret key generation rates. Ultimately, significantly reducing the computational resources required, by at least 99.99%, without affecting results accuracy, by up to 99.99%.

The impact of pretraining data on the ability of large language models to perform in-context learning has been largely unexplored. For example, it was not known how the way a model was trained affects its ability to learn new patterns without seeing them during the process, and how the content of the pretraining data influences this. This study investigates these questions by analyzing the performance of various open-source models in different inference settings and finding that the composition of the pretraining data has a significant impact on in-context learning ability. Specifically, models trained on more diverse and extensive data tend to excel at learning new patterns in a range of tasks, such as finding hidden relationships between numbers. In contrast, models trained on more limited data sets may show superior performance on specific types of tasks within those broader datasets. In order to gain deeper insights, the researchers developed a new framework that breaks down the pretraining data into different categories and evaluates each model's ability to use patterns from specific subsets of the data to improve its ability to handle real-world problems. This study not only sheds light on the importance of understanding how a model was trained in order to use it effectively, but also highlights the need to design data sets that can help researchers better assess the true capabilities of different models.

Galaxy cluster observations have primarily focused on the formation of central cold clouds and associated star formations, but little is known about the processes that create these clouds or their effects on star formation elsewhere in the cluster. To address this gap, researchers have developed a multi-dimensional and physically comprehensive simulation of a galaxy cluster to investigate these processes. Their results show that a pre-existing cold cloud can fragment due to Rayleigh-Taylor instability, producing smaller clouds through radiative cooling and growing through the accretion of hot gas. Meanwhile, turbulent motions within the cluster's hot atmosphere generate and heat additional cold clouds. These simulations reveal that magnetic field strength and orientation impact a fragment's development, while external magnetic fields tend to constrain its growth, and internal fields heat the surrounding environment. Furthermore, magnetic field strength and structures also influence particle acceleration, while more complex magnetic field topologies or the presence of heat transport mechanisms can increase a cold cloud's temperature.

The examination of $C\!P$ violation in beauty and charm enters an exciting era
as the DataseteX approach introduces an innovative methodology for analyzing
experimental data and conventional standards. The meticulous monitoring of
standard models and precision measurements facilitate enhancements in
knowledge. The Xeadark platform presents an innovative concept for providing a
comprehensive platform of analyses and tools for evaluating $C\!P$ violation
data across beauty and charm experiments.

New high-energy string interactions have been discovered in 10D open superstring theory. These amplitudes are unique as they are the only non-zero ones at specific thresholds. Calculations were done using two methods: a recursive approach based on insertion relations from string theory and perturbation in superstring amplitude. Their results are identical, leading to the conclusion that the amplitudes are accurately computed. Their properties were then analyzed, revealing they support an amplitudes-based suggestion first put forward by Gross many years ago. This, in turn, supports the all-order conjecture of Berends-Gieszterak for higher-order string scattering amplitudes. Additionally, it's discovered that at specific instances, their result is consistent with the work of Kawai-Lewellen-Tanaka rules as applied to superstring interactions. Finally, an explanation is given on why this approach works.

To effectively manage the vast amounts of data being generated by a growing number of mobile and IoT devices, future mobile networks (MNs) will require significant reconfiguration. To alleviate the burden on network operators, researchers have proposed the implementation of self-organizing, self-managing MNs, thereby reducing operational expenses and enhancing sustainability. This study presents an overview of managerial procedures in MNs, focusing on key aspects such as load balancing, energy optimization, and security to facilitate the deployment and operation of MaaS-based 5G networks. Additionally, the paper suggests that integrating core MN functions with edge computing could lead to innovative solutions for addressing critical MN challenges.

The objective of zero-speech synthesis is to create a speech synthesis technique that enables the transformation of written text into corresponding spoken voice, even without requiring related audio samples.  Building upon earlier work in zero-shot speech synthesis, this study delves into two crucial aspects: identifying acoustic features and designing interpolation strategies.  By examining the correlations between textual and acoustic data, it becomes evident that traditional features such as formants are hard to apply due to their simplified representation.  This research introduces a novel approach that involves clustering acoustic features without prior knowledge, which results in the identification of more effective features for improving synthesis quality.  Through detailed analysis, the influence of different numbers of clusters on the total variance and the coherence of the clusters is explored.  While variations in cluster counts may serve different applications, using around 500 clusters appears to yield the best overall results.  A multi-linear interpolation technique is employed to combine principal component analysis projections of the clustered forms, which leads to significantly improved synthesis quality compared to using separate instances trained for each speaker.  This study showcases the creation of a dataset utilizing natural speech samples and synthetic speech, enabling the evaluation of the proposed synthesis method against real audio examples.

Optimizing multi-limbed robots' motion is a challenging non-convex problem.
We approach this issue by creating an optimization framework that incorporates robot physics and uses personalized constraints to balance efficiency and feasibility in the optimization process.
Initially, we convert robot dynamics into a time-discrete form suitable for optimization and then introduce flexible constraints to manage the trade-off between finding a solution and obtaining an optimal one.
These constraints, derived from correlation analysis between simulation data and execution times, are applied based on real-time execution patterns to refine the optimization.
Our algorithm precomputes critical parameter ranges, including input and output variables, to implement this optimization strategy.
In addition, we developed a method for quickly evaluating the effectiveness of this strategy by simulating the optimization's gradient without running it.
Through thorough testing, we demonstrate the method effectively addresses the convolution of non-convexity and computational complexity in robotic physics optimization.

We have developed two innovative techniques for evaluating the probability of quantum state transformations using a specified resource. The first technique involves deriving a lower bound on the minimum probability of successful transformation by considering the distance between the target state and its closest possible state achievable without the resource. The second technique for obtaining an upper bound probability resembles a transform and tilt method. With these techniques in hand, we have successfully applied them to various quantum resource simulations, including the creation of quantum discord, reductions in Purview noise, and the restoration of quantum correlations. The results show that our methods are particularly useful in scenarios where quantum effects are minimal.

When a cup of coffee is accelerated, the surface reacts by changing shape, the underlying fluid dynamics similar to that of an elliptical pendulum, the fluid's motion self-organizing into a stable pattern, the shape of the surface related to that of a pendulum in a specific potential, the frequency of this stable pattern harder to predict due to a high degree of nonlinearity in the system.

In our research, we address the challenge of a regularized distributionally robust learning problem in decentralized networks by incorporating the Wasserberg distance to ensure robustness against data distribution shifts. By reformulating the problem in a simpler form, we propose a new distributed optimization algorithm combining the decomposed problem with the extragradient method and the decentralized accelerated solver. This innovative algorithm, specifically DR-DSGD, effectively addresses the complex decoupling issue and demonstrates, through theoretical analysis, its convergence rate and performance guarantee. We validate our approach through both simulated and real-world distributed network datasets, showcasing its superior performance compared to existing decentralized and distributed robust learning methods.

We utilize the concept of hydrodynamic attractors to establish a universal relationship between initial energy fluctuations and the number of particles produced in high-energy collisions. By employing a one-dimensional model and solving Boltzmann's equation through a kinetic theory approach, we demonstrate that particle production follows a universal pattern when normalized by the square of the energy density at a specific time, regardless of configuration. This outcome implies a fundamental connection between a system's initial energy fluctuations and its final particle distribution.

This study investigates the optimal equilibrium between performance capabilities and operational limitations for a specific category of nonlinear systems, encompassing balanced command filtered backstepping (BCFB) and balanced performance control (BPC). A novel approach involves introducing a performance safety assessment (PSA) metric that measures the distance between the current system state and its potential maximum reachable state within given constraints. Based on this PSA metric, a balanced control design adapts control parameters according to the current system state, ensuring optimal performance when constraints are minimal and prioritizing saturation point avoidance when constraints expand. Simulation results confirm the proposed approach surpasses an established control method, providing both enhanced performance and increased safety.

This research project seeks to establish a comprehensive understanding of how the solar radiation pressure influences orbital dynamics. For this purpose, a research team has developed a novel expression for the acceleration caused by solar radiation pressure, which is then utilized to identify and analyze the characteristics of solar resonances. These resonances mark the occurrence of exact alignments between the rotating elliptic orbit and the rotating mean anomaly, a crucial aspect of orbital behavior. Building upon existing analytical frameworks, our analysis builds on the work of Sturaro et al. and Lapwood in order to investigate the occurrence and frequency of solar resonances, which have significant implications for the stability and evolution of celestial bodies in the solar system. Utilizing both mathematical estimation and numerical simulation, our study aims to provide valuable insights into solar resonances, which can aid in the prediction and exploration of various aspects of orbital mechanics, including those related to boundary integrals in the context of mean-motion resonances.

We examine how first-principle tight-binding models of light-matter interactions depend on the chosen electromagnetic gauge. Our research shows that similar results can be obtained across different gauges, provided the same physical assumptions are used in all gauges. We demonstrate this gauge equivalence using the velocity and Coulomb forms of the Houbolt-Prada model, showing that the original formulation's inclusion of vertex enhancement avoids the need for additional terms, regardless of the gauge selected. Our findings also reveal that the differences between the frequency and time domains result in distinct physical assumptions, rather than being simply different methods of representation.

In a problem focused on category-level perception, we consider utilizing sensor data to identify and understand objects within specific categories despite variations within those categories. An active shape model, where pre-defined CAD models of various objects are used as a reference, is employed to derive the geometric shape and positioning of an object based on this model. Our perception algorithm's performance relies heavily on selecting the correct reference model, and its robustness is tested by examining the effects of model mismatch and measurement errors on the estimated shape and pose. Additionally, we discuss strategies for improving robustness through alternative algorithms and prior knowledge of the object's position and form. Finally, we present initial findings from our analysis of these issues using real-world data for bird classification.

We will define a confidence area for parameter estimates of a sample of size $N$ derived from random variables following a Cauchy distribution. By considering the Cauchy distribution's parameters as a single complex parameter, combining location $\mu$ and scale $\sigma$ as $\gamma = \mu + i\sigma$, we will determine a region within the complex plane, ultimately defining it as both a disc and a square using a straightforward formula.

A new statistical method is developed for basket trials to assess the effectiveness of a new treatment in multiple patient subgroups under a pre-defined safety and efficacy criteria. The results of each subgroup are combined into an overall measure of treatment efficacy, which is then compared to non-inferiority standards. A statistical framework is created that allows information to be shared between subgroups in terms of treatment effect correlations and overall efficacy uncertainty. Based on these principles, posterior distributions for overall treatment efficacy are calculated using pre-trial forecasts, enabling sample sizes to be determined based on certain confidence levels. The approach is validated through simulations and applied to a real trial dataset, resulting in determined sample sizes that are compared with those obtained through a statistical method that doesn't allow borrowing of information. The study demonstrates the effectiveness and flexibility of this new approach for setting trial requirements in multi-arm clinical trials.

To satisfy the rising demands of high-throughput in the industry, advanced motion systems must now be designed with a delicate balance between high-speed operation and high_precision.  By utilizing motion control structures that are flexible and adaptable to varying operating conditions, we can achieve performance optimization across a wide range of speeds and loads.  In this work, we explore the potential of using gain_ scheduled Linear Parameter Varying (LPV) controllers to optimize system performance under different conditions. Our approach involves developing LPV models to represent flexible dynamics, then creating corresponding LPV controllers to ensure robust stability under various operating conditions. Furthermore, we optimize the LPV weighting functions to minimize performance limitations, before transitioning to a sequential loop closing strategy to further enhance motion control system performance. Experimental validation is performed using a high_precision linear motor stage to verify the effectiveness of our proposed control method.

We introduce a general, flexible framework called Partial Registration Network (PRNet), designed specifically for aligning partial point cloud views. Building on learning-based registration methods, PRNet employs deep networks to overcome complex alignment and correspondence issues. Unlike existing methods that require a complete scene or extensive training data, PRNet can handle multiple viewpoints and a limited amount of training data. Our approach retains the scalability of learning-based techniques while addressing the limitations associated with complex scenes and varying views. Experimental validation on standard datasets demonstrates that PRNet outperforms existing learning-based methods and is second only to the top-performing fully observable methods.

A group G exhibits property $R_\infty$ if all automorphisms $\varphi$ of G produce an infinite number of twisted conjugacy classes. Finitely generated nilpotent groups possess this characteristic. We demonstrate that quotients of generalized solvable Baumslag-Solitar groups by their commutator subgroups are finitely generated nilpotent groups, which implies they exhibit property $R_\infty$. Moreover, the faibisheva-isonenko theorem states that certain BS-n groups have abelianizations that are finitely generated nilpotent groups; specific cases include Faibisheva-isonenko groups $i_n(G)$ that map onto direct sums of infinite cyclic groups.

Instead of presuming particular novel physics, we consider a range of potential solutions to cosmological and particle physics problems and calculate their potential impacts on collider experiments. Using this method, we evaluate the physical quantities that would be affected by each possible solution at various colliders and determine which specific collider experiment would be most effective in verifying the standard model's instability. For many of these hypothetical scenarios, the Large Hadron Collider with a luminosity 10 times higher than currently expected and the Future Circular Collider in its electron-meson and electron-positron forms appear to be most suitable. However, solutions rooted in extra dimensions, dark sector interactions, or Higgs portal mechanisms reveal that these theoretical frameworks could also be thoroughly investigated with present-day colliders such as the Large Electron-Positron, International Linear Collider, and Compact Linear Collider. Additionally, some solutions suggest that new physics might be within the reach of less powerful machines.

A new technique is developed to process time-sensitive data from ultra-fast experiments using an approach based on optimization in a pathway framework. This technique is successfully tested on data from experiments involving X-ray scattering and electron diffraction to analyze the breakdown of molecules. Results from applying the technique accurately match experimental findings and highlight key molecular movements, further aligning with other independent experimental evidence. What's more, this approach effectively considers the continuity of molecular structures and is resilient against noisy data.

We present the results of the first calculations of the longitudinal and transverse light-front distribution amplitudes for several mesons, specifically $D^*$, $D^*_s$, $\rho$, $\phi$, $K^*$, and $J/\Psi$. This calculation also yields distribution amplitudes for vector mesons, adhering to the CFKL classification. Our results for various mesons, when compared with experimental data, demonstrate consistency with a standard chiral phase. Additionally, the distribution amplitudes of the $J/\Psi$ meson were computed at varying radial excitation levels, showing the presence of node structures in their wave functions.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. The text further explores how the restriction of Schwartz functions to one-dimensional subspaces relates to the definition of ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$. Additionally, sufficient and necessary conditions are established for a particular type of Toeplitz operator to map ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$ functions onto itself.

Segmentation of unseen imaging modalities has been a difficult task due to a significant lack of available labeled data. Recent studies have shown that CycleGAN-based approaches can improve the accuracy of segmentation difficulty metrics by leveraging easy-to-acquire unlabeled data, making them highly suitable for medical applications. This research takes the concept a step further by applying CycleSegGAN directly to instance segmentation tasks, utilizing CycleSegGAN to generate more realistic object backgrounds from single images. CyclicSegGAN employs cyclic consistency loss based on the segmentation module and an object averager to generate reusable object backgrounds. Additionally, the architecture features a shared encoder between the forward and reverse generators, enabling efficient learning with limited supervisory input. CycleSegGAN has demonstrated improved performance over previous difficult-to-acquire segmentation tasks when evaluated on the Pascal VOC 2007 dataset for car instance segmentation. Notably, the proposed approach required significantly less training data – just 30% of the dataset – to achieve comparable results. Furthermore, CycleSegGAN has showcased promising results on real-world data, by successfully segmenting instances on MRI images.

Our proposed algorithm, Feature Mapping RNN, leverages key concepts in machine
learning, including the kernel trick and ReLU activations, to efficiently extract
dynamic features from arbitrary input data, allowing for accelerated
computation. The extracted features are then processed by an analysis RNN with
orthogonal weights, ensuring stable and efficient learning. An innovative approach
to estimating the model's hidden state by directly predicting a weighted sum of
tapped hidden states minimizes the depth of the network, resulting in a notable
reduction in parameters. This novel design is demonstrated to achieve superior
performance compared to existing methods in action anticipation.

Deep observations of active stars are crucial in identifying and understanding their magnetically driven mass ejections and high-energy flares. These events can serve as small-scale analogs for solar and stellar phenomena. AD Leo is a highly active Taurus complex star known for its extreme activity levels and rapid rotation. This study focuses on AD Leo's most intense flare ever recorded in the UV range since 1993. Using UV continuum fluctuations, we were able to map the inner coronal loop geometry, measure physical parameters, and estimate energy release during the event's peak. The findings indicate a temperature of 20-25 million Kelvin and a density range, 10^10.5 to 10^11.5 cm^-3, which suggests an active loop area and photospheric density. The energy analysis using Chandara's model proposed a power-law electron distribution, with a pitch index of 3.5, fulfilling stability requirements in the star's active region.

We are exploring the deformation theory of G2-instantons on nearly G2-manifolds. A one-to-one connection exists between nearly parallel G2 structures and real Killing spinors. Upon establishing the deformation complex for general G2-instantons, we discovered the association between the first cohomology space of the deformation complex and the first long exact sequence stemming from the spectral sequence of the twisted spinor complex. Additionally, we define the obstructions to the abelian and non-abelian deformations of general G2-instantons and also identify the second obstruction. Finally, we establish the deformation theory for the nearly parallel G2 structure.

A bounded linear operator $T$ on a complex Hilbert space with a countable basis is referred to as C-normal if it satisfies a particular condition under the action of a conjugation operation. Specifically, $T$ can be said to be C-normal if the product of $T$ and $U$ equals the product of $T$ and $U$. This concept can be applied to the study of composition operators in the context of function spaces. For a given analytic function $\phi$ on the open unit disc, the composition operator $C_{\phi}$ is defined as the operator that maps $f$ to $f \circ \phi$. Similarly, a weighted composition operator $W_{\psi,D}$ is defined for an analytic function $\psi$ and a linear operator $D$ as the operator that maps $f$ to $\psi(Df)$. This framework allows for the investigation of the spectral properties of these operators under the action of the conjugation operation.

This paper delves into a type of partition that excludes elements divisible by p. Specifically, the study targets p-core p'-partitions which adhere to these constraints. Notably, the largest of these p-core p'-partitions can be modeled by a long walk through a p-vertex graph, with edges assigned via the modulo p addition rule. Moreover, the research identifies a system for generating an extensive collection of these p-core p'-partitions.

Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation and industrial robotics, where geometric precision is critical. However, these models often suffer from noise when trained on 3D data and may distort underlying data distributions due to over-smoothing. While standard techniques like dropout have limitations in addressing this issue, our research focuses on developing an effective dropout technique for point cloud models. We propose a novel multi-affine dropout that targets different transformations of point clouds. This is in contrast to conventional methods like global noise, uniform dropout, or per-point noise, which introduce noise solely based on the point's position. By leveraging the invariance of point cloud models to standard geometric transformations like scaling and rotation, our model achieves better results. It combines affine transformations on individual points with scene-specific transformations. Our model acts as a lightweight regularizer without introducing additional parameters. Experimental results on shape recognition and dimension estimation demonstrate its superiority over baseline models.

We're investigating medium access techniques in Frequency-Modulated Continuous-Wave (FMCW) radar networks with all radar units utilizing identical settings, such as sweep duration and frequency characteristics. FMCW systems, often employed in large quantities for diverse applications, can be deployed in diverse settings like agricultural environments or urban parking facilities. We're analysing the performance metrics (like successful transmission rates and system efficiency) of two Medium Access Control methods: Slotted ALOHA and Carrier Sense Multiple Access with Exponential Backoff (CSMA-ED). Our research considers the challenges posed by neighboring targets and interference from other radar systems in our model.

Recent experiments have demonstrated the capability of using nonlinearity to manipulate quantum entanglement, which is typically viewed as a purely quantum phenomenon. We have mathematically examined the impact of entangled two-photon absorption on a widely used quantum interference experiment known as the Hong-Ou-Mandel interference experiment. This investigation reveals that the effects of linear and nonlinearity-induced phase shifts on the interference pattern differ, leading to variations in the phase and intensity within the experiment, ultimately altering the two-photon absorption probability. Notably, our findings show that an adjustable phase shift can compensate for the absorption contribution and restore the characteristic Hong-Ou-Mandel interference pattern. Furthermore, two-phase-shifter configurations have been identified that either eliminate or amplify the effects of two-photon absorption, resulting in complete absorption or enhanced absorption when compared to the original scenario. This property may offer potential applications for quantum information processing.

We calculate rational T-equivariant elliptic cohomology of complex projective spaces derived from finite dimensional T-representations V. This is accomplished by establishing that the T-equivariant elliptic cohomology theory constructed in Gre05, and the T^2-equivariant theory constructed in Bar22, share a key decomposition. This key decomposition facilitates reducing the T-equivariant cohomology computation to T^2-equivariant cohomology of complex spheres.

Temporal knowledge graph completion has emerged as a leading approach for
inferring accurate and missing event and temporal knowledge graph information.
Building upon successful applications of tensor decomposition in static graph
completions, we introduce TimeLR, a simple yet effective extension of the
traditional low-rank representation model that incorporates temporal knowledge
graph data. Building upon model-agnostic representations, we utilize embedding
vectors for head/tail timestamps and event/eventType entities along with their
corresponding dynamic relational matrices. To evaluate our model, we conducted
experiments on the standard datasets FC15, FC18, TC11/TC14, TC14/TC15/TC16/TC17/
TC18/TC19/TC20_UGC, TC14_IBM. The results show that our model performs
comparably to leading graph completion benchmarks such transR and transE under
baseline scenarios.

In the field of rigid body grinding, the interaction between the ground and the磨介 has so far been overlooked and treated only as a supportive force for media motion. To address this, we developed a ground sound model, incorporating the effects of media impact on the ground, using a coupled ground-media stiffness and damping spring system. By combining numerical simulations with experimental sound measurements, we validated our model. Analysis via sound energy spectrum and the sound intensity level index revealed that specific media shapes lead to a notable increase in sound intensity. Furthermore, our findings indicate that media impact generates a distinct high-frequency sound, differing from the traditional air-borne sound produced during grinding processes.

A concept known as Bell nonlocality without inequalities has been shown to occur in the network scenario of a tripartite source, specifically demonstrating how local realism can be outperformed even with imperfect correlations among the parts. 
We have refined this phenomenon and identified optimal measurement settings that make Bell nonlocality without inequalities possible under strict conditions. 
Experiments implementing these settings have been successfully conducted using photons, confirming the non-locality of the phenomenon. 
Notably, our findings reveal that partial correlations arise from optimal settings at a threshold of 85% correlation quality, whereas a full set of four required correlations is only achievable with 95% correlation. 
To overcome challenges in verifying Bell nonlocality using photons, we developed new sources producing high-fidelity entangled states and achieved significant improvements in correlation quality over previous experiments. 
Our results demonstrate a clear instance of Bell nonlocality without inequalities, characterized by optimal measurement settings enabling the occurrence of this phenomenon.

In flat band systems, constrained environments result in atypical behaviors influenced by randomness, indicating a need for further examination. We study the impact of random interactions on three-dimensional flat band systems, specifically the cubic lattice's fully polarized state. Our findings align with the predictions of the mean-field ansatz, revealing that the critical randomness threshold is an intricate combination of the magnetic hyperangle and the disorder strength. A new methodology is introduced for systematically addressing flat band disorder through generalized band filling in flat band systems, with applications to further complexities such as random couplings and multiple spin states.

A newly created hydrogen boride monolayer, existing in the Cmmm phase, exhibits potential as a superconductor due to similarities with MgB2 and an abundance of hydrogen within its structure. Utilizing density functional theory, the superconducting transition temperature of this material was estimated at around 15-20 K via the Allen-Dynes modified McMillan formula, based on calculations of its electronic and phononic properties. Nevertheless, the relatively low predicted transition temperature may not be sufficient for significant technological applications.

Research on the division of integers into equal parts reveals that the count of partitions with the same number of components follows a Bell curve pattern. Building upon this finding, we examine the behavior of a related sequence, which represents the distribution of partition lengths when all partitions are arranged in a grid by size. We prove that this distribution is multimodal and exhibit specific mathematical properties it possesses. Our analysis shows that as the integer value increases, the distinct peak counts rise linearly, while the peak areas remain consistent. Furthermore, these properties can also be observed in a subset of partitions, known as partitions with a specific number of components, which, when all such partitions are considered for each integer value, also display an 8-symmetric matrix pattern in their run lengths.

We categorize and understand a specific aspect of attractiveness in certain groups that occur when numbers are used in local fields, focusing on their characteristic weights. We demonstrate that if a group has certain properties related to symmetry and complexity, then these characteristics are both necessary and sufficient for the group to be understood through a specific mathematical framework that uses representations. We also study the possibilities of extending a specific type of mathematical framework that uses descriptions to groups that manage characteristics, determining which conditions are needed for this extension. We establish constraints on the existence of a group that is manageable and have implications on its ability to deform its representations.

Highly automated driving systems designed to operate in case of failure demand robust architecture and contingency planning mechanisms. To safeguard against unintended consequences, it's recommended that these systems disengage the driver when detected human inaction, triggering a chain of responsibilities extending to the automobile manufacturer, who must prioritize human safety by either design or instruction. Given the complexity of verifying such systems using traditional testing and analysis methods, a fail-operational driving system is formally described, validated, and verified using separation separation logic and higher-order proof, followed by an exploration of potential improvements through design enhancements.

Identifying clusters in complex systems with numerous interconnected components is a pressing challenge. Within each group, interactions are strongly interconnected, whereas connections between different systems are relatively weak. Utilizing machine learning techniques, we have developed an algorithm to discover these hidden relationships in complex systems automatically. By analyzing the impact of one part of a system on another, our method groups interconnected components and effectively identifies strongly interconnected subsystems. Tested on both linear and nonlinear systems, the algorithm successfully identified clusters and can recover previously known networks. Additionally, we have applied our algorithm to real-world data from brain activity and a study of infectious disease spread to demonstrate its ability to uncover strong connections within complex systems.

Recent research into Leibnizian calculus has centered on evaluating different fundamental approaches to describe its mathematical account. This study contributes to that research by formalizing and comparing the steps of mathematical account within the mathematical structure, using two existing frameworks (Enatski and Tedder's multivariable mathematical account framework and Morris's multistep mathematical account framework) to demonstrate the procedures of calculus. The investigation also examines the implications of making mathematical accounts versus conceptual frameworks.

We obtain theoretical predictions for the HI 21-cm emission of galaxies using a perturbation theory expansion, validated by N-body simulations with a baryonic feedback model. By comparing the model to HI intensity mapping data obtained from simulations, the effects of foreground removal are assessed. The model demonstrates a good match with the simulated HI 21-cm emission on scales larger than $1 \Mpc$. However, the predicted hiemba model underestimates the simulated data on smaller scales, likely due to inaccurate halo mass estimates for small-group halos. The hiemba model fails to reproduce non-linear effects that enhance the 21-cm power spectrum's amplitude at low multipoles. Additionally, hiemba significantly differs from simulates the hiemba model's 21-cm emission spectrum on scales between $5 \Mpc$ and $30 \Mpc$. By analyzing hiemba's 21-cm emission spectrum, one can establish the minimum sufficient halo physics to accurately represent HI 21-cm emission, given that hiemba significantly differs from simulates the hiemba model's 21-cm emission spectrum, the hiemba model's 21-cm emission spectrum, and its hiemba model's 21-cm emission spectrum.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the bias-variance equilibrium utilizing supplementary information. In particular, methods incorporating text-based document modeling have significantly improved accuracy by incorporating inherent data variability. Nonetheless, these models are prone to overfitting in the context of ample data and heightened complexity. Our innovative text-aware hybrid system integrates both context-driven and behavior-centric recommender techniques to mitigate the drawbacks of variational models and address the issue of data sparsity. Our advanced context-driven approach utilizes advanced document modeling incorporating semi-specified features. We semi-automatically identify the most impactful attributes using unsupervised feature learning methods. Meanwhile, our streamlined hybrid scheme simplifies the integration of context-based and behavior-based recommender systems. Our thorough experimentation using real-world datasets demonstrates the efficacy of our innovative solution in enhancing overall accuracy while effectively minimizing variability.

Using common tools from random matrix theory, we demonstrate how to derive significant results about the independence relationships within matrices with independent entries. We apply this approach to prove the freeness and conditional freeness principles for matrices of the forms $X\oplus -X$ and $U X U^* + U^* X^* U$, where $U$ represents a random unitary matrix.

This paper revisits monitoring real-time systems by leveraging properties described either in Metric Interval Temporal Logic or as Timed B\"uchi Automata. We propose effective, symbolic, and online monitoring methods in several contexts that take advantage of 'zones', a concept familiar from efficient model checking of Timed Automata. These contexts encompass improved treatment of timing discrepancies, monitoring under timing ambiguity, and the extension of monitoring to provide earliest time estimates for when decisive verdicts can be rendered.

The decay reactions $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi
a_0(980)$ are examined in detail. Attention is focused on the potential impact of
the vector-axialvector transition on the production of $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$. A new
production mechanism for $f_0(980)$ is identified, with possible consequences for
determining the isoscalar parameters defining the $f_0(980)$ and $a_0(980)$ states.

The GRAVITY acquisition camera utilizes four distinct optical paths to pinpoint the precise location of a celestial source with high sensitivity. Its intricate design, featuring a spider web structure, ensures accurate source localization. In an effort to enhance its performance, a comprehensive study was conducted to determine the high-resolution image of a celestial source by solving an inverse problem. By employing a range of sophisticated techniques, a groundbreaking result was achieved, resulting in a high-resolution image with a resolution of 0.4 mas. The resulting image demonstrates a remarkable improvement of over 30% compared to the GRAVITY camera's intrinsic resolution. The resulting image quality is equivalent to a field of view roughly one-third the size of its current field. The resulting image confirms that the GRAVITY acquisition camera can effectively operate at near-infrared wavelengths while maintaining a large field of view. The resulting image also reveals that the GRAVITY acquisition camera can effectively detect a highly focused source at approximately three times the diffraction limit, while maintaining an effective field of view one-third the size of its current field. The resulting image also reveals that the GRAVITY acquisition camera can effectively operate at near-infrared wavelengths, even when attempting to detect a highly focused source at approximately three times the diffraction limit, while maintaining a field of view approximately one-third the size of its current field.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs of reduced doubling and highway dimension. Our study reveals that problems with a constant number of forbidden subsets (doubling dimension) admit a logarithmic approximation, while those with a larger number of such subsets (highway dimension) allow only for constant approximations. This distinction mimics the behavior observed in Euclidean space, where low-dimensional problems yield logarithmic approximations and higher-dimensional ones constant approximations. We provide a recipe to convert a constant-factor approximation for $k$-Center with a fixed number of parameters, and investigate the complexity of related problems. We solve these problems, except for the $l$-Cover problem which is shown to be NP-hard even with $l=3$, while $k$-Set Cover remains open. We derive a new upper bound of $o(k)$ on the set cover complexity, and explore lower bounds via extended hardness assumptions. Additionally, we develop an approximation scheme based on clustering and consider the applicability to doubling and highway dimension. We introduce the $k$-Set Cover problem and discuss its applicability to doubling and highway dimension.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire solution of the equation $\Delta_{\eta}^{m}f-Q_1=(\Delta_{\eta}^{k}f-Q_{2})e^{P}$ exhibits hyper-order with the same degree as the polynomial $P$, and based on this result, we establish the differential difference counterpart to Bruck's conjecture. Furthermore, we have successfully proved Bruck's conjecture for the specific instance where the hyper-order of $f$ is less than $\frac{1}{2}$.

This research paper explores solving polynomial linear systems in the presence of errors using an evaluation-interpolation technique, with a focus on minimizing the number of computations required to recover the solution. This is crucial because it depends on parameters like the degrees and size of the systems, as well as the error rate. A key aspect of this study is that it assumes a random error distribution over a large field, which simplifies the problem. This paper improves the existing bounds on the minimum number of computations needed in this scenario. Specifically, for balanced and worst-case error rates, new and lower bounds are established using an information-theoretic approach. This lower bound is then used to design a new algorithm that achieves the best results. This algorithm incorporates a novel early termination technique, allowing for an even more efficient process. Moreover, this paper shows that solving such systems with very low error rates using the current method still involves significant work, highlighting the need for further research.

In the ultrastrong coupling regime of cavity QED, we show that the parity symmetry of the system leads to a protected quantum light emission, with photons emitted only from specific parts of the cavity. This phenomenon is exemplified in a planar cavity design, where the parity symmetry causes coupled excitons to exist in a hybrid state. Distinguishable bundle-like photons emitted from the cavity are controlled by the excitations of the two corners, which are governed by the system's parity symmetry. The parity symmetry protection is further验证ed by both theoretical calculations and experimental data, which also show that perturbations to the system's structure preserve the protected photon emission, as long as the parity symmetry remains intact.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 5 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements.

In the context of vector-meson dominance model, properties of light vector mesons in local parity breaking mediums with chiral imbalance are explored. By utilizing a finite lowest-order local effective Lagrangian derived from QED, an analysis of the quadratic Vector Meson Dominance model amplitude is conducted. This results in a medium where chiral imbalance induces a phenomenon where the mass of vector mesons splits into two, characterized by the mixing of vector and axial vectors. Notably, this phenomenon is driven by the quantum nature of chiral fermion charges.

We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be arbitrarily close to 1. For comparison, prior work has established that estimating a standard graph's edge count requires at least Omega(n^(1+delta)) degrees of freedom, illustrating the estimation problem's intrinsic difficulty. Additionally, we discuss how estimation relates to the problem of locating a typical node in the network, and we identify specific conditions under which this task is impossible for distant nodes. We also highlight that this impossibility result applies to an idealized, perfectly connected network with no errors.

In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be resolved to determine the metric variables of the spatial slice and extrinsic curvature. Our novel approach modifies the standard conformal transverse-traceless method by introducing an additional degree of freedom, removing the assumption that the Hamiltonian constraint is initially satisfied. By introducing this assumption as an extra equation with an associated function, we gain the ability to propose four different variants of this method.

The Jiangmen Undeveloped Neutrino Observatory project, located in China, plans to deploy a large liquid scintillator and detect neutrinos using an advanced photodetector system consisting of roughly 30,000 20-inch photo-multipliers. Following the success of the day/night rate measurement goal met by the previous phase of the project, additional research will focus on determining the nuclear fuel cycle's difference between enriched and de-enriched uranium. With the need for an even greater number of photodetectors, the project will prioritize obtaining high-quality units at a more affordable price. Consequently, a production line was established in collaboration with multiple Chinese institutions to create around 30,000 PMTs annually. This article discusses the production methods and quality testing and characterization methods applied to these photodetectors.

In recent years, deep learning models, specifically Recurrent Neural Networks and Long Short-Term Memory networks, have been the top choices for time series prediction. However, they struggle with large input outputs and are prone to the overfitting issue. Convolutive approaches, on the other hand, have shown better scalability but are less capable of handling long dependencies in the data. Recent innovations in Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory and Multilayer Perceptron-Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory networks have addressed these limitations. Despite their improvements, these models are still limited by their inability to handle long dependencies effectively and their inability to prevent overfitting in complex scenarios.

Our research aims to develop an adaptive framework that combines the strengths of Graph Convolutional Networks in capturing long dependencies, a normal unit in regulating model complexity, and Convolutional LSTM in refining the features within each layer. Our proposed model, called MGUC, shows significant performance gains over state-of-the-art models on both synthetic and real-world datasets, with the best results achieved on the Air Quality Index and the S&P 500 Index.

Astronomical observations from the Atacama Desert are heavily impacted by atmospheric dispersion due to the site's geographical location, which can distort and distort starlight across different wavelengths. To minimize this effect, astronomers employ atmospheric dispersion correctors (ADCs) in conjunction with adaptive optics (AO) systems to restore a galaxy's intrinsic shape. To effectively synchronize the adjustments required, it is crucial to have a precise understanding of the atmospheric dispersion, which can be achieved through detailed analysis. We analyzed data from the Atacama Desert using the UVIS unit telescope of the Extremely Large Telescope (XLTE) to characterize the atmospheric dispersion. To minimize errors associated with the galaxy's shape and size, we carefully selected specific conditions, which included using bright, point-source stars. To eliminate the influence of optical aberrations, we utilized baffle systems to remove the distorted outer segments of the galaxy's image. To eliminate the effects of the galaxy's intrinsic shape, which varied based on the choice of filter set, we carefully analyzed the images under various conditions.
